start.heading: The spine
items: Time → States → Payoffs → Prices → Portfolios → No-arbitrage → SDF (L1 “big picture”).

Fixed income = the SDF along the time axis: zero price P(T) = E[mt+T] → coupon bonds are portfolios of zeros (LOOP) → spot rates, YTM and forwards are translations of zero prices → duration and convexity measure how prices move when discounting changes.

Equity = the same pricing equation with an infinite, growing payoff: P = E[m(P + D)] → DDM → Gordon P = D/(R − g), growth g = ROE·b, value created only if ROE > R (PVGO). Valuation ratios are rearrangements of it: D/P = R − g, P/E = 1/R + PVGO/E; Campbell–Shiller shows they mostly forecast returns.

Uncertainty made explicit: states → random variables → (conditional) expectations → prices. MPT is the investor’s problem with risk measured by variance: portfolio arithmetic → diversification leaves only systematic risk → CAL / tangency portfolio → mutual fund theorem. CAPM: markets clear, so the market portfolio is the tangency portfolio and expected returns depend on β. That is a restriction on the SDF, m = a − bRM: all priced risk is one-dimensional. Anomalies and the Roll critique motivate multiple factors.
Everything else is a definition built from these, a convention for measuring them, or a consequence of two rules (prices are linear; no free lunch).
“Prices are disciplined by arbitrage, interpreted through risk, and sometimes explained by equilibrium.”

clusters.title: CAPM II — beta, the SDF & empirics

T.label:
Time
t = today → t+1, t+2, …
details: Finance = trading resources today for outcomes in the future.
Today is t; future dates are t+1, t+2, t+3, …
Prices are dated when they are paid. Payoffs are dated when they are received.

S.label:
States of the world
s = 1, …, S
details: Symbols: s = index of a state; S = number of states.
A set of S mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive future states (boom/recession, high/low inflation, good/bad).
Each state is a complete description of all economically relevant outcomes at that date.
A label for a possible future: a bookkeeping device, not a prediction.

PR.label:
Probabilities πs
πs #gt; 0, Σ πs = 1
details: Symbols: π<sub>s</sub> = probability of state s.
A convenient way to summarize uncertainty over states.
No-arbitrage pricing restrictions do not need them; they first appear when the SDF is built.
Different choices of π give different (equivalent) SDF representations.

X.label:
Asset ≡ payoff vector
X = (X1, …, XS) ∈ ℝS
details: Symbols: X<sub>s</sub> = payoff in state s; X<sub>i,s</sub> = payoff of asset i in state s; ℝ<sup>S</sup> = a list of S real numbers (one payoff per state).
A contract that trades at t and delivers a payoff at a future date, contingent on the realized state.
X<sub>i,s</sub> is the payoff of asset i in state s. It is what you get, not what you pay.
Assets are defined by their payoffs, not their type: stocks, bonds, options and insurance differ only in what they pay and when.
Payoffs can have any sign. A negative X<sub>s</sub> means you must pay in state s.
Long and short positions are allowed. A short flips every sign: (−2, 5, 10) becomes (2, −5, −10).
Shapes: a risk-free bond pays the same in every state. A stock pays more in good states. Insurance pays more in bad states. An option pays 0 in some states and > 0 in others.

P.label:
Price P(X) ∈ ℝ
paid today
details: The amount paid today to receive the future payoff. A real number assigned to a list of state-contingent payoffs.
Prices are observable; future payoffs are uncertain.
Financial economics studies the relationship between prices today and payoffs tomorrow.
Prices and payoffs are the primitive objects of theory. Returns are what we analyze in data.

RFX.label:
Risk-free payoff
Xs = 1 in every state
details: Symbols: X<sub>s</sub> = payoff in state s; P<sub>t</sub> = price today; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.
The same payoff in every state. Its gross return is 1 + R<sub>f</sub> = 1/P<sub>t</sub>, so P<sub>t</sub> = 1/(1 + R<sub>f</sub>).

SNOT.label: A state is NOT a forecast
details: States and probabilities are analytical devices, not forecasts or beliefs.

RET.label:
Simple return
1 + R = Xt+1 / Pt
details: Symbols: R = net simple return (1 + R is the gross return); X<sub>t+1</sub> = payoff next period; P<sub>t</sub> = price today; P<sub>t+1</sub> = price next period; D<sub>t+1</sub> = dividend paid next period.
Stock payoff: X<sub>t+1</sub> = P<sub>t+1</sub> + D<sub>t+1</sub> (next price plus dividend).
Gross simple return: 1 + R<sub>t+1</sub> = (P<sub>t+1</sub> + D<sub>t+1</sub>)/P<sub>t</sub>. Net: R = X/P − 1.
A measurement convention derived from prices and payoffs. A higher return means more earned per dollar invested.
Annualizing is conventional: periods are usually years.

LOG.label:
Log return
r = ln(1 + R)
details: Symbols: r = log (continuously compounded) return; R = simple return; ln = natural log.
Not a different economic object: the same payoff in different units, like meters instead of feet.
Used because logs add over time, not because investors think in logs.
For small R, ln(1 + R) ≈ R.

MP.label:
Multi-period (compound) return
1 + Rt,t+2 = (1 + Rt+1)(1 + Rt+2)
details: Symbols: R<sub>t+1</sub> = return from t to t+1; R<sub>t+2</sub> = return from t+1 to t+2; R<sub>t,t+2</sub> = compound return from t to t+2.
Hold from t to t+1, reinvest dividends, hold to t+2.

LADD.label:
Log returns add over time
rt,t+2 = rt+1 + rt+2
details: Symbols: r<sub>t+1</sub>, r<sub>t+2</sub> = one-period log returns; r<sub>t,t+2</sub> = log return from t to t+2.
Logs turn products into sums. This is the whole reason log returns are used.

AM.label:
Arithmetic mean
Σ Ri / n
details: Symbols: R<sub>i</sub> = return in period i; n = number of periods.
Describes the expected single-period return.
There is no single “average return”. Each average answers a different question.
AM.example: Returns 30% then 0%: arithmetic mean = 15%. But 15% twice compounds to (1.15)² − 1 = 32.25%, while 30%-then-0% gives only 30%.

GM.label:
Geometric mean
[Π (1 + Ri)]1/n − 1
details: Symbols: R<sub>i</sub> = return in period i; n = number of periods; Π = product; r<sub>i</sub> = ln(1 + R<sub>i</sub>); r̄ = average log return.
Solves (1 + R)ⁿ = Π(1 + R<sub>i</sub>). It describes the multi-period growth rate along the realized path.
In logs it is just the plain average: r̄ = (r<sub>1</sub> + … + r<sub>n</sub>)/n.

EAR.label:
Effective annual rate
EAR = (1 + APR/m)m − 1
details: Symbols: APR = quoted annual rate; m = compounding periods per year (⚠ not the SDF m); EAR = rate actually earned over a year.
Interest credited m times per year: bank accounts daily, mortgages and leases monthly, bonds semi-annually.
The quoted APR R differs from the EAR you actually earn or pay.
EAR.example: $10,000 car loan at a 6.75% APR, compounded daily: EAR = (1 + .0675/365)<sup>365</sup> − 1 = 6.9824%. You owe $10,698.24 after one year.

CC.label:
m → ∞: 1 + EAR = er
continuous rate = log rate
details: Symbols: R = quoted annual rate (APR); m = compounding periods per year; e ≈ 2.718; r = continuously compounded (log) rate.
lim (1 + R/m)<sup>m</sup> − 1 = e<sup>r</sup> − 1, so r = ln(1 + EAR) is the continuously compounded rate, also called the log rate.
This is a limit, not how assets actually pay. It is used because it turns products into sums and powers into exponentials.
Notation: capital R is a periodically compounded rate; lowercase r is a continuously compounded rate.
CC.example: Car loan compounded continuously: e<sup>.0675</sup> − 1 = 6.9830% → $10,698.30 (vs $10,698.24 daily).

INF.label:
Inflation
1 + πt+1 = CPIt+1 / CPIt
⚠ this π ≠ probability πs
details: Symbols: π<sub>t+1</sub> = inflation rate from t to t+1; CPI<sub>t</sub> = consumer price index at t.
Measures the change in the purchasing power of $1. CPI = the average price of an urban consumer basket (BLS).
π > 0 is inflation; π < 0 is deflation.
⚠ Notation clash: π is also used for state probabilities. Context tells you which.

RX.label:
Real payoff
Xreal = X / (1 + π)
details: Symbols: X = nominal payoff (dollars); π = inflation rate; X<sup>real</sup> = payoff in today's purchasing power; W<sub>t+1</sub> = wealth next period.
Measures the payoff in today’s purchasing power. The notes first show this with wealth: W<sup>real</sup><sub>t+1</sub> = W<sub>t+1</sub>/(1 + π).
Nominal change in wealth (dollars) ≠ change in purchasing power.

REAL.label:
Real return
1 + Rreal = (1 + Rnom) / (1 + π)
details: Symbols: R<sup>nom</sup> = nominal (dollar) return; R<sup>real</sup> = real return; π = inflation rate; X<sup>real</sup> = real payoff; P<sub>t</sub> = price today.
1 + R<sup>real</sup> = X<sup>real</sup>/P<sub>t</sub>. Only the payoff is deflated; the price is already in today’s dollars.

H.label:
Holdings a = (a1, …, aN)
shares, long (+) or short (−)
details: Symbols: a<sub>i</sub> = number of shares of asset i held (negative = short); N = number of assets.
You can hold many assets at once, buying some and shorting others.

PF.label:
Portfolio = linear combination
Xp,s = Σ aiXi,s · Pp = Σ aiPi
details: Symbols: a<sub>i</sub> = shares of asset i; X<sub>i,s</sub> = payoff of asset i in state s; X<sub>p,s</sub> = portfolio payoff in state s; P<sub>i</sub> = price of asset i; P<sub>p</sub> = portfolio price.
Portfolio payoffs and prices are weighted sums of the individual pieces.
Mutual funds (e.g. Vanguard) are portfolios.

ACC.label:
Linearity here is accounting,
not an economic assumption
details: Because payoffs literally add, prices of combinations must add too. This is what the pricing rules in ④ formalize.

W.label:
Portfolio weights
wi = aiPi / Σ ajPj
details: Symbols: w<sub>i</sub> = weight on asset i; a<sub>i</sub> = shares held; P<sub>i</sub> = price of asset i, so a<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub> = dollars in asset i.
The share of wealth in asset i. The weights sum to 1.

RPF.label:
Portfolio return = weighted average
Rp = Σ wiRi
details: Symbols: R<sub>p</sub> = portfolio return; R<sub>i</sub> = return on asset i; w<sub>i</sub> = weight on asset i; a<sub>i</sub> = shares; X<sub>i</sub> = payoff; P<sub>i</sub> = price of asset i.
R<sub>p</sub> = (portfolio payoff at t+1)/(portfolio price at t) − 1.

Write (Σ a<sub>i</sub>X<sub>i</sub>)/(Σ a<sub>j</sub>P<sub>j</sub>) = Σ [a<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub>/Σ a<sub>j</sub>P<sub>j</sub>]·(X<sub>i</sub>/P<sub>i</sub>). This gives 1 + R<sub>p</sub> = Σ w<sub>i</sub>(1 + R<sub>i</sub>), so R<sub>p</sub> = Σ w<sub>i</sub>R<sub>i</sub>.
It works for simple returns because payoffs add. It does NOT hold for log returns.

IDX.label: Index = portfolio + weight rule
details: A portfolio meant to represent the general market. It is described by which securities it holds and the weights on them.

PW.label:
Price-weighted
wi = Pi / Σ Pj
details: Symbols: w<sub>i</sub> = weight on stock i; P<sub>i</sub> = its share price; Σ P<sub>j</sub> = sum of all prices in the index.
E.g. the Dow Jones Industrial Average (30 large U.S. stocks).

VW.label:
Value-weighted
wi = Vi / Σ Vj, Vi = niPi
details: Symbols: w<sub>i</sub> = weight on stock i; V<sub>i</sub> = its market cap; n<sub>i</sub> = shares outstanding; P<sub>i</sub> = share price.
V<sub>i</sub> = market cap (n<sub>i</sub> = shares outstanding). More money goes into bigger companies.
E.g. Russell 1000, Russell 2000.

FF.label:
Free-float weighted
value-weighted minus locked-up shares
details: Like value-weighted, but excludes shares held privately or by the government.
E.g. the S&P 500 (500 large-cap U.S. firms: the large-cap segment, not the whole market) and the MSCI foreign-stock indexes.

EW.label:
Equal-weighted
wi = 1/N
details: Symbols: w<sub>i</sub> = weight on asset i; N = number of assets.
Equal dollars in each asset. E.g. the S&P 500 Equal Weight and Nasdaq-100 Equal Weighted indexes.

PWR.label:
Price-weighted ⇒ equal number of shares
index tracks the sum of prices
details: Symbols: W = dollars invested; P<sub>i</sub> = price of stock i; ΣP = sum of prices.
Shares of i = (P<sub>i</sub>/ΣP)·W/P<sub>i</sub> = W/ΣP, the same for every stock.
PWR.example: $100; Historic $40 (100 sh outstanding), Present $20 (50 sh). Price-weighted: 40/60 and 20/60 → $66.67 and $33.33 → 1.67 sh of each. Equal-weighted: $50/$50 → 1.25 and 2.5 sh. Value-weighted: caps 4000 : 1000 → $80/$20 → 2 and 1 sh.

NOREB.label:
Price- & value-weighted:
buy-and-hold, no rebalancing
details: Prices move the held shares’ values exactly as they move the index weights, so the portfolio stays on target by itself.

REB.label: Equal-weighted ⇒ must rebalance
details: Price moves push the weights away from 1/N.
REB.example: Next year Historic $45 and Present $33: holding 1.25 and 2.5 sh, the weights drift to .4054 and .5946 (value $138.75). To get back to 1/2 each: 69.375/45 = 1.54 sh and 69.375/33 = 2.10 sh.

R1.label:
Rule 1 · prices add
P(X + Y) = P(X) + P(Y)
details: Symbols: X, Y = payoff vectors; X<sub>s</sub>, Y<sub>s</sub> = their payoffs in state s; P(·) = price today.
Buying both assets pays (X<sub>1</sub>+Y<sub>1</sub>, …, X<sub>S</sub>+Y<sub>S</sub>) and costs the sum of the prices.

R2.label:
Rule 2 · prices scale
P(aX) = a P(X), a ∈ ℝ
details: Symbols: X = payoff vector; a = a real number (number of units); P(·) = price.
Buy twice as much and you get twice the payoff in every state: P(2X) = 2P(X).

P0.label: P(0) = 0
details: P(X + 0) = P(X) + P(0), so P(0) = 0. A zero payoff has zero price.

LIN.label:
Linear pricing (through the origin)
P(aX + bY) = aP(X) + bP(Y)
details: Symbols: X, Y = payoff vectors; a, b = real numbers (units held); P(·) = price.
The first crucial modeling implication: rules 1 and 2 combined.

ARB.label:
Arbitrage (free lunch)
X ≥ 0 in every state and P(X) #lt; 0,
or X ≥ 0, some Xs #gt; 0 and P(X) ≤ 0
details: Symbols: X = payoff vector of the trade; X<sub>s</sub> = its payoff in state s; P(X) = its price today (negative = you are paid).
A trade that never loses money in any state and either pays you today or costs nothing and pays off in at least one state.
Case (i) includes the all-zero payoff: being paid today to receive nothing.
Intuition: it costs nothing, never loses, and sometimes makes money.

NA.label:
No-arbitrage
no such X exists
details: Theory assumes arbitrage opportunities do not exist. The usual motivation is that they would be eliminated very quickly.
A basic consistency requirement: prices cannot allow free lunches.

NANOT.label:
NOT a behavioral claim, not about trader
skill or market speed; needs no preferences,
beliefs or equilibrium
details: It is purely a logical restriction on which prices are allowed.

POS.label:
Positive pricing
X = 0 ⇒ P = 0 · X ≥ 0, X ≠ 0 ⇒ P(X) #gt; 0
details: Symbols: X = payoff vector; P(X) = its price; X ≥ 0 means no negative payoff in any state.
“This is the entire content of no-arbitrage.” In this setting no-arbitrage and positive pricing are equivalent.

LOOP.label:
Law of One Price
X = Y state by state ⇒ P(X) = P(Y)
details: Symbols: X, Y = payoff vectors of two assets; P(·) = price.
Prices depend only on payoffs, not on asset labels.
If LOOP fails, buy the cheap one and sell the expensive one for a riskless profit.
A consequence of no-arbitrage, not a separate rule.

AD.label:
Arrow–Debreu security es
pays 1 in state s, 0 elsewhere
details: Symbols: e<sub>s</sub> = Arrow–Debreu security for state s (payoff 1 in state s, 0 elsewhere); s = state index.
A way of organizing prices. Such securities need not literally trade.

Q.label:
State price qs = P(es)
today’s value of $1 in state s
details: Symbols: q<sub>s</sub> = state price of state s; e<sub>s</sub> = Arrow–Debreu security for state s; P(·) = price.
“How much is a dollar worth in each future state?”

SPR.label:
State-price representation
∃ q1, …, qS #gt; 0 : P(X) = Σ qsXs
details: Symbols: q<sub>s</sub> = state price of state s (today's price of $1 in s); X<sub>s</sub> = payoff in state s; S = number of states; ∃ = there exist.
If prices are linear and rule out arbitrage, every asset price is a positively weighted sum of its state payoffs.
Not an assumption: with finitely many states and linear prices, this is the only form prices can take.
Existence comes from no-arbitrage. It does not say why each q<sub>s</sub> has the value it does.

COMP.label:
Complete market
traded assets can build any payoff
details: Symbols: P<sub>i</sub> = price of traded asset i; X<sub>i,s</sub> = its payoff in state s; q<sub>s</sub> = state price; S = number of states; ℝ<sup>S</sup> = space of all possible payoff vectors.
Any pattern of payoffs across states can be created from traded assets.
Equations vs unknowns: each traded asset gives one equation Pi = Σs qsXi,s, and there are S unknowns q1…qS. Complete means S independent equations, so exactly one solution.

Linear algebra: the payoff vectors span ℝS (rank S). That needs S independent assets, not that every asset is independent. A redundant asset, like a fund of other assets, adds no new equation; LOOP already fixes its price.
COMP.example: 2 states. Bond (1, 1) costs 0.95; asset A (1.2, 0.8) costs 0.92. Then q<sub>1</sub> + q<sub>2</sub> = 0.95 and 1.2q<sub>1</sub> + 0.8q<sub>2</sub> = 0.92 give q = (0.40, 0.55) and nothing else.

INC.label:
Incomplete market
some payoffs cannot be built
details: Symbols: q = (q<sub>1</sub>, …, q<sub>S</sub>) state-price vector; t = free parameter indexing the family of valid q's (⚠ not time).
Fewer independent payoff vectors than states, so fewer equations than unknowns and a whole family of q’s.
Real markets are generally incomplete.
INC.example: 3 states. Bond (1, 1, 1) costs 0.90; stock (0, 1, 2) costs 0.80. Set q<sub>3</sub> = t; then q<sub>2</sub> = 0.8 − 2t and q<sub>1</sub> = 0.1 + t, and positivity requires 0 #lt; t #lt; 0.4. For example, t = 0.1 gives q = (0.2, 0.6, 0.1) and t = 0.3 gives q = (0.4, 0.2, 0.3). Both price the bond and the stock exactly.

REPL.label:
Every AD security can be replicated
⇒ each qs is forced by LOOP
details: Symbols: q<sub>s</sub> = state price of state s; (1, 0) = payoff $1 in state 1 and nothing in state 2.
This is why completeness gives uniqueness. Build $1-in-state-s from traded assets; its price is qs, and any other q would let you arbitrage the replicating portfolio.

UNQ.label:
q is unique
(pinned down by asset prices)
details: Symbols: q = state-price vector.
Exactly one state-price vector is consistent with all observed asset prices. The data leaves no freedom.
Existence ⇐ no-arbitrage. Uniqueness ⇐ completeness.
The pricing rule then extends to every contingent claim (PS2 Q7b).

UNOT.label:
“Unique” does NOT mean “true” or
“correct”, only pinned down by the data
details: Symbols: q = state-price vector.
Uniqueness is a statement about how much observed prices restrict q, not about whether those prices are “right”.

MANY.label: Many q fit observed prices
details: Symbols: q = state-price vector.
Several state-price vectors are consistent with the same prices, so the market cannot tell them apart.
This matters only for payoffs you cannot build (see the two nodes below).

SPAN.label:
Buildable payoffs: one price
under every valid q
details: Symbols: q = state-price vector; (2, 1, 0) = payoff in states 1, 2, 3.
Anything in the span of traded assets has a single price that LOOP forces. Every member of the q family agrees on it.

BOUND.label:
Unbuildable payoffs: only a range
(no-arbitrage bounds, not a number)
details: Symbols: q<sub>s</sub> = state price of state s; t = free parameter of the q family (⚠ not time).
If a payoff cannot be replicated, its price depends on which q you pick. No-arbitrage (all q<sub>s</sub> #gt; 0) still restricts it to an interval.
BOUND.example: 3-state example: the AD security (1, 0, 0) costs q<sub>1</sub> = 0.1 + t with 0 #lt; t #lt; 0.4, so anywhere in (0.1, 0.5).

M.label:
Stochastic discount factor
ms = qs / πs
details: Symbols: m<sub>s</sub> = SDF value in state s; q<sub>s</sub> = state price; π<sub>s</sub> = probability of state s.
Built from state prices and probabilities. Also called the state-price density or pricing kernel.
A state-contingent weight vector that summarizes how prices weight payoffs across states, i.e. how risk is priced.
All asset pricing models differ only in how they specify, interpret or estimate m.

PEQ.label:
Pricing as an expectation
P(X) = Eπ[mX] = Σ πsmsXs
details: Symbols: P(X) = price; X<sub>s</sub> = payoff in state s; m<sub>s</sub> = SDF in state s; π<sub>s</sub> = probability; q<sub>s</sub> = state price; E<sub>π</sub> = expectation using probabilities π.
Substitute q<sub>s</sub> = π<sub>s</sub>m<sub>s</sub> into P = Σ q<sub>s</sub>X<sub>s</sub>.
Given π, this is an equivalent representation of no-arbitrage.

MVAL.label:
ms = how much the market values $1 in s
high m ⇒ “bad” state, payoffs worth more
details: High m<sub>s</sub>: dollars in state s are more valuable. Low m<sub>s</sub>: less valuable.
Payoffs delivered in high-value states get more weight in pricing.
This reading uses only prices and no-arbitrage, with no assumptions about behavior.

MNOT.label:
m is NOT a probability, a price,
a belief, a return, or a utility function
details: It is a weight vector, nothing more.

MU.label: m is unique (given π)
details: Symbols: q = state-price vector; π = probability vector; m = SDF.
A complete market fixes q uniquely; any choice of π then fixes m uniquely.

MM.label:
m is not unique
⇒ approximate one that prices assets well
details: Even under the true probabilities, markets are generally incomplete, so the SDF is not pinned down.
Setting π = the true measure only selects one representation among many that generate the same prices.
Empirical asset pricing therefore aims to approximate an SDF that prices observed assets well.

STRUCT.label:
Arbitrage says q exists, not why qs
is what it is ⇒ need economic structure
details: Symbols: q<sub>s</sub> = state price of state s.
Even in a complete market, arbitrage does not explain the economic content of the SDF.

IMRS.label:
IMRS reading
ms,t+1 ∝ u′(cs,t+1) / u′(ct)
details: Symbols: m<sub>s,t+1</sub> = SDF in state s at t+1; u′(c) = marginal utility of consumption c; c<sub>t</sub> = consumption today; c<sub>s,t+1</sub> = consumption in state s next period; ∝ = proportional to.
The intertemporal marginal rate of substitution: how preferences value an extra unit of payoff across dates and states.
m is high where marginal utility is high.
Preferences help interpret the SDF; they do not determine it.

RQ.label: 1 = E[m(1 + R)]
details: Symbols: m = SDF; X = payoff; P(X) = price; R = net return, so 1 + R = X/P(X).
Divide P(X) = E[mX] by P(X) and use X/P(X) = 1 + R.

ERQ.label: E[1 + R] = 1/E[m] − Cov(m, R)/E[m]
details: Symbols: m = SDF; R = net return; Y, Z = any random variables.
Use Cov(Y, Z) = E[YZ] − E[Y]E[Z]: 1 = E[m]E[1 + R] + Cov(m, 1 + R), and Cov(m, 1 + R) = Cov(m, R).
“The core pricing intuition of the entire course: prices reward assets for delivering payoffs in valuable states.”

RFR.label: E[m] = 1 / (1 + R<sub>f</sub>)
details: Symbols: m = SDF; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.
Price the risk-free payoff: 1/(1 + R<sub>f</sub>) = E[m·1]. Here m prices payoffs at t+1 relative to t.

PREM.label:
Risk premium
E[R] − Rf = −Cov(m, R) / E[m]
details: Symbols: E[R] = expected return; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate; m = SDF; π<sub>G</sub>, π<sub>B</sub> = probabilities of the good and bad state.
Substitute 1/E[m] = 1 + R<sub>f</sub> and subtract 1 + R<sub>f</sub> from both sides.
PREM.example:
Two states, πG = πB = ½, m = (0.8, 1.1), so E[m] = .95 and Rf = 5.26%.
Asset A pays (1.2, 0.8): P = .5(.8·1.2 + 1.1·.8) = 0.92; 1 + R = (1.3043, 0.8696); E[R] = 8.70%; Cov(m, RA) = −.0326.
Asset B pays (0.8, 1.2): P = 0.98; 1 + R = (0.8163, 1.2245); E[R] = 2.04%; Cov = +.0306.
Both have E[X] = 1. Their prices differ only because of which state pays.

RISK.label: Risk ≡ covariance with m
details: Risk is about how payoffs line up with bad states of the world.
Assets earn higher expected returns if they perform poorly when times are bad, or make bad outcomes worse.

RNOT.label:
Risk is NOT variance / volatility per se,
and NOT downside risk by itself
details: Two assets with the same volatility can carry opposite risk premia (see the A/B example).
CAPM II: what matters is how an asset co-moves with the market portfolio; beta is a normalized measure of that covariance.

SIGN.label:
Cov #lt; 0 (pays when m low) ⇒ E[R] #gt; Rf
Cov #gt; 0 (pays when m high) ⇒ E[R] #lt; Rf, insurance-like
details: Symbols: m = SDF; R = asset return; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.
Negative covariance: the asset pays off where an extra unit is least valuable, so it must offer a premium (asset A).
Positive covariance: the asset pays off where an extra unit is most valuable, so it can offer less than R<sub>f</sub> (asset B).
The link between “m low” and “good times” holds “under mild assumptions”.

FI.label:
Fixed income
contractual cash flows at specified dates
details: Assets that promise contractually specified cash flows at specified dates: Treasuries, corporate bonds, mortgages, MBS/CMOs, ABS/CDOs, and derivatives on these.
Cash flows are dated (timing matters) and often state-contingent in practice.
Markets quote yields and spreads, which are different representations of prices.
Not a niche: global debt is roughly $140–150T, versus $120–130T of global equity.

DATED.label:
Dated pricing equation
Pt(Xt+T) = Et[mt+TXt+T]
details: Symbols: P<sub>t</sub>(·) = price at t; X<sub>t+T</sub> = payoff at t+T; m<sub>t+T</sub> = SDF for horizon T; T = horizon; E<sub>t</sub> = expectation given information at t.
The SDF pricing equation with a second dimension, horizon T. m<sub>s,t+T</sub> = how much we value a dollar in state s at t+T.
Prices are dated when paid, payoffs when received (core objects). Interpretation is identical to the one-period SDF.

ZERO.label:
Zero-coupon bond
pays face value at t+T, nothing before
details: Symbols: T = years to maturity; t = today.
Characterized by a face value, a maturity date t+T and a price at t. No cash flows until maturity.
The risk-free zero with face $1 pays $1 in every state at t+T: a dated sure dollar.
U.S. Treasuries are the closest real-world example: default-free in nominal terms, highly liquid, the benchmark. Treasury bills (≤ 1 yr) are zeros; stripped Treasuries (STRIPS) give longer zeros.

ZP.label:
Zero price = SDF mean at horizon T
Pt(T) = Et[mt,t+T]
details: Symbols: P<sub>t</sub>(T) = price at t of a zero paying $1 at t+T; m<sub>t,t+T</sub> = SDF from t to t+T; E<sub>t</sub> = conditional expectation at t.
The primitive term-structure object. Every other fixed-income quantity (spot rates, yields, forwards, duration) is built from or summarizes these prices.
The spot curve is therefore a collection of SDF moments at different horizons.

RFS.label:
Short rate
1 + Rf = 1/Pt(1) = 1/Et[mt+1]
details: Symbols: R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate (short rate); P<sub>t</sub>(1) = price of the one-period zero; m<sub>t+1</sub> = one-period SDF; S<sub>1</sub> = one-year spot rate.
The one-period zero’s gross return is the gross risk-free rate, also called the short rate. It comes from the mean of the SDF.

RFI.label: High E[m] ⇒ safe $ tomorrow is dear ⇒ low R<sub>f</sub>
details: Symbols: E[m] = mean of the SDF; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.

A safe dollar tomorrow becomes more valuable when tomorrow looks worse, riskier or harder to insure against: bad economic news (recession risk, lower income, negative productivity), higher uncertainty (crises, geopolitical shocks, pandemics), tighter borrowing (credit crunches, banking stress), or more demand for safety (demographics, regulation).
Then demand for safe claims rises, they cost more today, and R<sub>f</sub> falls. Low E[m] works the other way.

LONGR.label:
“Risk-free” long bond is still risky
if sold before maturity
details: “Risk-free” means no default risk: held to maturity it surely pays $1.
Before maturity its price depends on discounting, which changes with (i) the time value of money and (ii) changing assessments of future states. So its one-period return is risky.
A long bond (maturity > 1 period) moves when the market’s valuation of future dollars changes. This is formalized as duration and convexity.

SPOT.label:
Spot rate ST
Pt(T) = 1/(1 + ST)T
details: Symbols: S<sub>T</sub> = T-year spot rate; P<sub>t</sub>(T) = price of a zero paying $1 in T years; T = maturity.
The constant per-period rate that matches the zero’s price: S<sub>T</sub> = (1/P<sub>t</sub>(T))<sup>1/T</sup> − 1.
Rates are quoted in practice, but all economic content lives in prices. Spot rates are a conventional way of reporting them.

SPC.label:
Spot curve
ST plotted against T
details: Symbols: S<sub>T</sub> = T-year spot rate; P<sub>t</sub>(T) = T-year zero price; T = maturity.
Summarizes how expensive it is today to buy sure dollars at different future dates. Equivalent object: the zero-coupon price curve P<sub>t</sub>(T) vs T.
Need not be monotone: it can slope up or down, be flat, or be humped (PS3: no-arbitrage does not force monotonicity; P(T) falls with T only if rates are nonnegative).

SPNOT.label:
Spot rates are NOT primitives:
a translation of zero prices
details: Symbols: P<sub>t</sub>(T) = T-year zero price; m<sub>t+T</sub> = SDF at horizon T; S<sub>T</sub> = spot rates.
Primitive: prices P<sub>t</sub>(T) (equivalently E<sub>t</sub>[m<sub>t+T</sub>]). Representation: spot rates {S<sub>T</sub>}.

CB.label:
Coupon bond
coupon C each period + face F at T
details: Coupon rate = C/F (quoted as a % of face). T = time to maturity.
Treasury notes: 1–10 years; Treasury bonds: > 10 years. Corporates (e.g. Nike) also carry ratings (Moody’s / S&P).

CBZ.label:
Coupon bond = portfolio of zeros
Pt = Σ CFs·Pt(s)
details: Symbols: CF<sub>s</sub> = cash flow at date s; P<sub>t</sub>(s) = price of a zero paying $1 at s; C = coupon; F = face value; T = maturity.
Hold C units of the 1-period zero, C of the 2-period, …, C + F of the T-period zero: identical cash flows at every date and state, so identical price.
No preferences or yields required; it follows directly from no-arbitrage. Coupon bonds introduce no new pricing logic.
The most transparent way to price a coupon bond.

SPP.label:
Spot-curve pricing
P = Σ CFs/(1 + Ss)s
details: Symbols: CF<sub>s</sub> = cash flow at date s; S<sub>s</sub> = s-year spot rate; P<sub>t</sub>(s) = s-year zero price; C = coupon; F = face.
A representation of Σ CF<sub>s</sub>·P<sub>t</sub>(s), not a new pricing rule. Each cash flow is discounted at its own maturity-specific rate.

ONEN.label:
One discount rate for all cash flows
is NOT how prices are set
details: Spot rates generally differ across maturities, so different cash flows are discounted differently. One rate hides which maturities drive value.
PS3: with an upward-sloping curve, discounting everything at the long rate over-discounts the early cash flows and understates the price.

YTM.label:
Yield to maturity R
P = Σ CFs/(1 + R)s
details: Symbols: R = yield to maturity (one rate for all dates); CF<sub>s</sub> = cash flow at date s; P = price.
The single number that reproduces the price: an internal rate of return, a summary of a price.
Not solvable analytically in general; found by root finding.
We care because markets quote yields, returns are reported in yield terms, and duration and convexity are defined in yield space. But yields always come after prices.

YNOT.label:
YTM is NOT a discount rate the market uses,
NOT a primitive, NOT tied directly to the SDF
details: “Spot rates price cash flows; yields summarize prices.”

ANN.label:
Level-coupon form
P = (C/R)(1 − (1+R)−T) + F/(1+R)T
details: Symbols: P = price; C = coupon per period; F = face value; R = yield to maturity; T = maturity.
Compact bond price when every cash flow is discounted at the single yield R.

PAR.label: Par bond: coupon rate = YTM ⇒ P = F
details: Symbols: P = price; C = coupon; F = face; C/F = coupon rate; R = yield to maturity.
Plug C/F = R into the level-coupon form and P = F.
Discount bonds: P < F (coupon rate < YTM). Premium bonds: P > F (coupon rate > YTM).

CONS.label:
Consol (perpetuity)
P = C/R
details: Symbols: P = price; C = coupon paid forever; R = yield.
No maturity and no terminal payment: take T → ∞ in the level-coupon form (assuming R > 0).

YC.label:
Yield curve / term structure
YTM plotted against maturity
details: A summary of bond prices, typically upward sloping but with many possible shapes.
“Term structure” can mean the on-the-run yield curve (most recently issued Treasuries) or the spot curve (from stripped Treasury prices). We price with the spot curve; yields come afterward.
Term-structure changes hit bonds differently depending on the timing of their cash flows: interest-rate risk.

DISC.label:
Discounting changes ⇒ zero prices move
(“rates move” is shorthand)
details: Symbols: P<sub>t</sub>(T) = T-year zero price; m<sub>t,t+T</sub> = SDF from t to t+T.
Reasons: expectations evolve (growth, inflation, risk), time passes, policy paths clarify, risk assessments change, preferences or technology drift, economic surprises.
The value of a future dollar can change even without surprises.
The primitive that moves is P<sub>t</sub>(T) = E<sub>t</sub>[m<sub>t,t+T</sub>]; spot rates move because they are defined from prices.
A coupon bond’s interest-rate risk is inherited from its zero components.

MD.label:
Modified duration
D* = −(1/P)·dP/dR
details: Symbols: D<sup>*</sup> = modified duration; P = bond price; R = yield to maturity; dP/dR = slope of price in yield.
A local sensitivity (a derivative), computed from cash flows and the yield-based price representation.
Converts a small change in rates into an approximate % change in price.

DAP.label:
Duration approximation
ΔP/P ≈ −D*·ΔR
details: Symbols: ΔP/P = % price change; ΔR = change in yield (decimal; 50 bp = 0.005); D<sup>*</sup> = modified duration.
First-order: price moves opposite to yields, scaled by D*. In dollars: ΔP ≈ −D*·P·ΔR.

MAC.label:
Macaulay duration
D = Σ s·ws, ws = [CFs/(1+R)s]/P
details: Symbols: D = Macaulay duration; s = date of a cash flow; CF<sub>s</sub> = cash flow at s; R = yield; P = price; w<sub>s</sub> = share of price coming from the cash flow at s.
A PV-weighted average maturity, sometimes called the bond’s “effective” maturity. The weights sum to 1.
Related to modified duration by D* = D/(1 + R).

DZ.label:
Zero: D = T, D* = T/(1+R)
coupon bond: D #lt; T
details: Symbols: D = Macaulay duration; D<sup>*</sup> = modified duration; T = maturity; R = yield.
Longer maturity ⇒ larger duration ⇒ more interest-rate risk.
Coupons pull cash flows forward, reducing the PV-weighted average maturity.
Concept check (FI II): a 5-yr zero is more sensitive to long-horizon discounting than a 5-yr coupon bond, because all its PV sits at t+5.

DPR.label:
Duration rules
↑ with maturity · ↓ with coupon · ↓ with yield
details: Symbols: TTM = time to maturity.

1. A zero’s Macaulay duration equals its TTM. 2. Same TTM: lower coupon ⇒ higher duration. 3. Same coupon: duration generally rises with TTM. 4. All else equal, duration is inversely related to yield.

PD.label: Portfolio D* = Σ (value weight)·D*<sub>i</sub>
details: Symbols: D<sup>*</sup><sub>i</sub> = modified duration of bond i; D<sup>*</sup><sub>A</sub>, D<sup>*</sup><sub>L</sub> = durations of assets and liabilities; $A, $L = their dollar values.
Given as a hint in PS4. Used to hedge: match dollar durations, D*<sub>A</sub>·$A = D*<sub>L</sub>·$L, so asset and liability values change by the same amount.

STB.label: Rate moves: shift · twist · butterfly
details: Shift: all spot rates move by the same amount (parallel). Twist: slope changes (short and long rates move opposite ways). Butterfly: curvature changes (short and long vs medium).
Under a parallel shift, longer-duration bonds move more. Under a twist or butterfly, it depends on where the bond’s PV sits across maturities.

EFD.label:
Effective duration
Deff = −(1/P)·(P+ − P−)/(2Δx)
details: Symbols: D<sub>eff</sub> = effective duration; P = current price; P<sub>+</sub>, P<sub>−</sub> = prices after shifting the spot curve up/down by Δx; Δx = size of the shift.

Shift the whole spot curve up and down by Δx, reprice to get P<sub>+</sub>, P<sub>−</sub>. Sensitivity to the primitive curve rather than to the derived yield; needs no single-yield representation. ΔP/P ≈ −D<sub>eff</sub>·Δx.
Shift, twist and butterfly durations are effective durations under the corresponding curve moves; they are central to bond risk management.

CONV.label:
Convexity
C = (1/P)·d²P/dR²
details: Symbols: C = convexity (⚠ not the coupon); P = price; R = yield; d²P/dR² = curvature of price in yield; s = cash-flow date; w<sub>s</sub> = PV weight (as in Macaulay duration).
Bond prices are nonlinear (typically convex) in yield, so duration is only first-order.
C = [1/(1+R)²]·Σ (s² + s)·w<sub>s</sub>, with the same PV weights as Macaulay duration.

DCA.label:
Second-order approximation
ΔP/P ≈ −D*ΔR + ½C(ΔR)²
details: Symbols: ΔP/P = % price change; D<sup>*</sup> = modified duration; C = convexity; ΔR = change in yield.
Adds the convexity correction to the duration line.
DCA.example: D* = 6, C = 60: ΔR = +1% ⇒ −0.06 + 0.003 = −5.7%; ΔR = −1% ⇒ +0.06 + 0.003 = +6.3%. Equal moves give asymmetric price changes.

CVI.label:
Positive convexity is desirable:
price falls less and rises more
details: The convexity term is always positive for plain bonds, so it helps the holder in both directions. It is tiny for small moves (10 bp) and matters for large ones (200 bp, PS4).

FWD.label:
Forward rate fs,T
(1+ST)T = (1+Ss)s(1+fs,T)T−s
details: Symbols: f<sub>s,T</sub> = forward rate from s to T (agreed today); S<sub>T</sub>, S<sub>s</sub> = spot rates for T and s years; s < T = dates.
Two strategies: buy a T-period zero, or buy an s-period zero and roll over for T − s periods. No-arbitrage equates them.

Many derivatives are written on forward rates: FRAs lock in a future rate, swaps exchange fixed for floating, caps and floors are options on future short rates. Forwards are the natural language of interest-rate risk.

FWP.label: f<sub>s,T</sub> = (P(s)/P(T))<sup>1/(T−s)</sup> − 1
details: Symbols: f<sub>s,T</sub> = forward rate from s to T; P(s), P(T) = zero prices for maturities s and T; S<sub>1</sub> = one-year spot rate.
Forward rates are determined entirely by zero prices. One-year forward: f<sub>s,s+1</sub> = P(s)/P(s+1) − 1; and f<sub>0,1</sub> = S<sub>1</sub>.

FNOT.label: f is NOT the expected future short rate
details: Symbols: f = forward rate.
The future short rate is uncertain at t, so the rollover strategy is risky.

TP.label:
f = Et[future short rate] + term premium
since Cov(m, Rroll) #lt; 0
details: Symbols: f = forward rate; E<sub>t</sub> = expectation at t; m = SDF; R<sub>roll</sub> = return on rolling over short-term zeros.
The rollover strategy tends to earn high returns in good states (low m) and low returns in bad states (high m), so it requires compensation. This is the risk-premium logic of L5 applied across time.

BR.label: Sources of bond risk (8)
details: Symbols: P&I = principal and interest; EDF = expected default frequency.
Interest-rate (market): price moves opposite to rates. Reinvestment: YTM assumes coupons are reinvested; interest-on-interest depends on future rates.
Call: issuer can retire early, so cash flows are uncertain, the bond is called when rates fall (reinvestment risk), and price upside is capped near the call price.
Inflation: purchasing power of cash flows. Exchange-rate: non-dollar bonds have uncertain dollar cash flows.
Liquidity: ease of selling near value; measured by the bid–ask spread. Volatility: higher rate volatility raises embedded-option value and lowers the bond’s value.
Default (credit): issuer can’t make timely P&I payments. Rated by S&P, Moody’s, Fitch; Moody’s also estimates expected default frequency (EDF).

BR2.label:
All bond risks = uncertain discounting
or uncertain cash flows
details: Interest-rate and reinvestment risk: discounting. Inflation and FX: real value of promised cash flows. Call and volatility: embedded options make cash flows state-contingent. Default: cash flows cut in some states. Liquidity: may not sell at fundamental value.

YSP.label:
Yield spread
x = Rcorp − RTreas
details: Symbols: x = yield spread; R<sub>corp</sub> = corporate bond yield; R<sub>Treas</sub> = yield on a comparable Treasury; CF<sub>s</sub> = cash flow at date s; P<sub>corp</sub> = corporate bond price.
The constant added to a comparable Treasury’s yield to reproduce the corporate bond’s price: P<sub>corp</sub> = Σ CF<sub>s</sub>/(1 + R<sub>Treas</sub> + x)<sup>s</sup>.
A Microsoft bond and a Treasury with the same maturity and coupon don’t sell for the same price: the corporate adds at least default and liquidity risk.

SSP.label:
Static spread
x added to the whole spot curve
details: Symbols: x = static spread; S<sub>s</sub> = Treasury s-year spot rate; CF<sub>s</sub> = cash flow at s; P<sub>corp</sub> = corporate bond price.
P<sub>corp</sub> = Σ CF<sub>s</sub>/(1 + S<sub>s</sub> + x)<sup>s</sup>. Like the yield spread, computable directly from observed prices.

OAS.label:
Option-adjusted spread (OAS)
model-based, for embedded options
details: The constant shift of the Treasury spot curve that makes a pricing model (which values the embedded option, e.g. a call) match the market price.
Model-dependent: not directly observable from price alone.

SPI.label:
Spread = every risk a Treasury doesn’t have
(default ≈ biggest part, but only a rough gauge)
details: The static spread and OAS are often just called “the spread”. A CDS price quantifies default risk more precisely.

CDS.label:
Credit default swap
insurance against default
details: Protection buyer pays a periodic premium; protection seller pays if a credit event occurs (bankruptcy/insolvency/payment default, a stipulated price fall, or a rating downgrade).
Payment: par minus post-default price, or par in exchange for physical delivery of the defaulted asset. Traded OTC (private contracts).

CDP.label:
One-period CDS
X = p(1 − Z) ⇒ p = X/(1 − Z)
details: Premium X paid up front; expected payoff p(1 − Z), with p = default probability and Z = recovery rate. X is set so the swap has zero value at inception.

MBS.label:
Mortgage-backed security
cash flows from a pool of mortgages
details: Symbols: P&I = principal and interest.

Banks sell mortgage loans (assets funded by deposits) to free up lending. Agencies (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac) pool them and sell the MBS; they backed ~70% of the market in 2023. Subprime was securitized privately without a guarantee.
Pass-through: all P&I passed to investors, minus servicing and guarantee fees.
Scale: ~$12–13T of MBS (≈ 20–25% of the U.S. bond market), vs Treasuries $25–27T, corporates $10–11T, munis $4–5T.

MBR.label:
MBS risks: default (agency-guaranteed)
+ prepayment: contraction / extension
details: Agency MBS investors are protected from homeowner default by the guarantee. All MBS investors face prepayment risk: contraction (prepayments speed up when rates fall) and extension (prepayments slow when rates rise).

CMO.label:
CMO: tranches paid principal in
order of seniority
details: Redistributes a mortgage pool’s cash flows across bond classes. All tranches get interest; principal goes to tranche 1 first, then 2, then 3.
Junior tranches absorb losses first; tranches differ in prepayment and extension exposure and are sold to investors with different risk appetites.

CMR.label:
Tranching reallocates risk;
total cash flow is unchanged
details: The tranche payoffs add up to the pool in every state.
CMR.example: Face 10 per tranche. Boom: pool 30 ⇒ (10, 10, 10). Recession: pool 15 ⇒ (10, 5, 0).

EQ.label:
Equilibrium
(Econ 139)
details: Add preferences, beliefs, endowments and market clearing to explain why prices arise.
It does not replace the no-arbitrage restrictions.

EMP.label:
Empirical asset pricing
(Econ 144)
details: Works with realized returns, factors, pricing errors and estimated SDFs.
Tests whether observed prices satisfy the theoretical restrictions.

MV.label:
Mean–variance
analysis
details: Summarizes assets by average return, volatility, and how they move together, instead of tracking every state.
Shows which risk–return combinations are feasible given prices. It describes feasible portfolios, not optimal choices.

EFF.label:
Information &
efficiency
details: Symbols: I<sub>t</sub> = information available at t.
Information I<sub>t</sub> restricts how predictable returns are. Efficiency claims are about conditional expectations.
Efficient markets can still be risky. Efficient does not mean prices are “right”.

STK.label:
Common stock
residual claim on the firm
details: An ownership claim on a corporation; payouts come as cash dividends or stock dividends.
Unlike bonds, payouts are uncertain in both magnitude and timing.
Shareholders are residual claimants on the firm’s assets after debt holders; liability is limited to the amount invested; they typically have voting rights.
Shares can be sold short in secondary markets.
Primary market: venture capital (private placement), IPO (first public issue), SEO (additional shares by a public firm), usually through an investment bank acting as underwriter.
Secondary market: shares trade after issuance on exchanges such as the NYSE and NASDAQ.

SPAY.label:
Stock payoff
Xt+1 = Pt+1 + Dt+1
details: Symbols: X<sub>t+1</sub> = payoff next period; P<sub>t</sub>, P<sub>t+1</sub> = price today and next period; D<sub>t+1</sub> = dividend next period; m<sub>t+1</sub> = SDF; E<sub>t</sub> = expectation given time-t information.
For a stock the payoff is next period’s price plus dividend, so pricing is still P<sub>t</sub> = E<sub>t</sub>[m<sub>t+1</sub>X<sub>t+1</sub>].
Nothing fundamental changes from fixed income: prices equal discounted expected payoffs. What changes is the payoff process.
In fixed income cash-flow timing was fixed and uncertainty entered mainly through discount rates; in equity the payoff itself evolves through reinvestment and growth.
Equity valuation separates two channels: growth of payoffs (productivity, reinvestment) and discounting of payoffs (risk and the SDF).
From bonds to stocks: maturity is infinite, cash flows are uncertain, and the discount rate reflects risk.

REQ.label:
Required return on equity R
set in financial markets
details: The discount rate in equity pricing; these notes hold it constant.
For aggregate equity R typically exceeds the risk-free rate, because investors require compensation for bearing systematic risk.
How differences in risk across assets show up as differences in R is deferred to asset pricing models.

ONEP.label:
One-period pricing
Pt = Et[Pt+1 + Dt+1]/(1 + R)
details: Symbols: P<sub>t</sub> = price today; P<sub>t+1</sub> = price next period; D<sub>t+1</sub> = dividend next period; R = required return on equity; E<sub>t</sub> = expectation at t.
Same logic as bond pricing: price equals discounted expected payoff.
R is the required return on equity.

TVC.label:
Terminal term vanishes
Pt+K/(1 + R)K → 0
details: Symbols: P<sub>t+K</sub> = price K periods ahead; K = number of periods iterated; D<sub>t+i</sub> = dividend i periods ahead; R = required return.
Iterating the one-period identity K periods gives P<sub>t</sub> = P<sub>t+K</sub>/(1+R)<sup>K</sup> + Σ<sub>i≤K</sub> D<sub>t+i</sub>/(1+R)<sup>i</sup>.
If the discounted terminal price goes to zero as K → ∞, only the dividend sum remains.

DDM.label:
Dividend discount model
Pt = Σ Dt+i/(1 + R)i
details: Symbols: P<sub>t</sub> = price today; D<sub>t+i</sub> = dividend i periods ahead; R = required return on equity.
Stock price equals the present value of future dividends.
Derived by assuming a constant R, writing P<sub>t</sub> = (P<sub>t+1</sub> + D<sub>t+1</sub>)/(1+R) (expectations suppressed), substituting forward and letting the terminal term vanish.
Practical challenge: it requires forecasting an infinite stream of dividends, hence the simplifying assumptions (constant dividend, constant growth).

NODIV.label:
Non-payers: Pt = Ps/(1 + R)s−t
value comes from later dividends
details: Symbols: P<sub>t</sub> = price today; P<sub>s</sub> = price at the later date s when dividends start; D<sub>s+i</sub> = dividends after s; R = required return.
The DDM holds at every date. If no dividends are paid between t and s, P<sub>s</sub> = Σ D<sub>s+i</sub>/(1+R)<sup>i</sup> and discounting back gives P<sub>t</sub>.
Even firms that pay no dividends today derive their value from dividends expected in the future.

DCONST.label: Constant dividend: P = D/R
details: Symbols: P = price; D = constant dividend each period; R = required return.
Assume D<sub>t+i</sub> = D for all i; the DDM sums to D/R.
This is identical to the pricing of a consol bond.

GGM.label:
Gordon growth model
Pt = Dt+1/(R − g), R #gt; g
details: Symbols: P<sub>t</sub> = price today; D<sub>t</sub> = dividend just paid; D<sub>t+1</sub> = next dividend; D<sub>t+i</sub> = dividend i periods ahead; R = required return; g = dividend growth rate.
Dividends grow at constant rate g: D<sub>t+i</sub> = D<sub>t</sub>(1+g)<sup>i</sup>.
Substituting into the DDM gives a growing perpetuity, which simplifies to D<sub>t</sub>(1+g)/(R − g) = D<sub>t+1</sub>/(R − g), provided R > g.

GSENS.label:
Small R − g ⇒ price very sensitive
to R and g
details: Symbols: P = price; D<sub>t+1</sub> = next dividend; R = required return; g = growth rate.
When R − g is small, small changes in either R or g move the price a lot.
This parallels duration: long-duration bonds are very sensitive to rate changes; high-growth stocks are very sensitive to discount-rate or growth assumptions.

GCAP.label:
Price grows at g
(Pt+1 − Pt)/Pt = g
details: Symbols: P<sub>t</sub>, P<sub>t+1</sub> = price today and next period; D<sub>t+2</sub> = dividend two periods ahead; R = required return; g = growth rate.
Under the GGM, P<sub>t+1</sub> = D<sub>t+2</sub>/(R − g) = P<sub>t</sub>(1+g): the stock price grows at the dividend growth rate.
So g is the capital appreciation rate.

RDEC.label:
R = Dt+1/Pt + g
dividend yield + capital appreciation
details: Symbols: R = required (expected) return; D<sub>t</sub>, D<sub>t+1</sub> = current and next dividend; P<sub>t</sub>, P<sub>t+1</sub> = price today and next period; g = growth rate.
From R = (P<sub>t+1</sub> + D<sub>t+1</sub>)/P<sub>t</sub> − 1 = D<sub>t+1</sub>/P<sub>t</sub> + g = D<sub>t</sub>(1+g)/P<sub>t</sub> + g.
D<sub>t+1</sub>/P<sub>t</sub> is the expected dividend yield; D<sub>t</sub>/P<sub>t</sub> is the current dividend yield.
The first term is the cash return; the second is the percentage price change.

DOWNOT.label:
Risky equity is NOT discounted
at the Treasury rate
details: Symbols: R = required return; g = growth rate; D/P = dividend yield; D<sub>t+1</sub> = next dividend.
Glassman and Hassett (1999) argued the DJIA at ~9,000 was four times too low using the GGM with R equal to the Treasury rate.
Treasuries pay off with near certainty while aggregate equity payoffs are risky, so required equity returns exceed Treasury yields.
The argument is extremely sensitive to the assumed R because price depends on the small difference R − g.

ROE.label:
Return on equity
ROE = Et+1/Kt
details: Symbols: ROE = return on equity; E<sub>t+1</sub> = earnings next period (⚠ not an expectation); K<sub>t</sub> = capital stock today.
Dollars earned per dollar invested; earnings are cash flow generated after operating costs.
K<sub>t</sub> is the capital stock: tangible and intangible assets (machinery, buildings, land, IP) the firm invested in to generate revenue.
ROE is determined by firm productivity and investment decisions.

RETN.label:
Retention ratio b
Dt+1 = (1 − b)Et+1
details: Symbols: b = retention ratio; D<sub>t+1</sub> = next dividend; E<sub>t+1</sub> = next period's earnings.
b is the fraction of earnings reinvested, so E<sub>t+1</sub>·b is reinvested and the rest is paid out as dividends.
Simplification: the firm is 100% equity financed, so all retained earnings add to the capital stock.

ROENOT.label: ROE is NOT R
details: Symbols: ROE = return on equity (firm's return on its capital); R = required return set by markets.
ROE comes from firm productivity and investment decisions.
R is the required return determined in financial markets.
The notes call this distinction essential: comparing the two decides whether reinvestment creates value.

GROW.label:
Growth from reinvestment
g = ROE · b
details: Symbols: g = growth rate; ROE = return on equity; b = retention ratio; K<sub>t</sub> = capital; E<sub>t+1</sub> = earnings next period.
K<sub>t+1</sub> = K<sub>t</sub> + b·E<sub>t+1</sub> = K<sub>t</sub>(1 + ROE·b), so capital grows at ROE·b.
Earnings (ROE·K<sub>t</sub>) and dividends ((1−b)·ROE·K<sub>t</sub>) are constant fractions of capital, so they grow at the same rate.
Reinvest everything (b = 1) ⇒ grow at ROE. Under the GGM the stock price also grows at ROE·b.

PGROW.label:
Price with growth
Pt = (1 − b)Et+1/(R − ROE·b)
details: Symbols: P<sub>t</sub> = price; b = retention ratio; E<sub>t+1</sub> = next earnings; R = required return; ROE = return on equity; g = ROE·b.
Substitute D<sub>t+1</sub> = (1−b)E<sub>t+1</sub> and g = ROE·b into the GGM.
Raising b has two effects: dividends fall (pushes price down) and growth rises (pushes price up).
If ROE < R the first dominates; if ROE > R the second dominates; if ROE = R they cancel and P<sub>t</sub> = E<sub>t+1</sub>/R.

RETB.label:
Retain if ROE #gt; R, pay out if ROE #lt; R
ROE = R ⇒ b doesn’t matter
details: Symbols: ROE = return on equity; R = required return; b = retention ratio.
ROE > R: projects beat alternative investments of similar risk, so management should retain earnings; higher b raises the share price.
ROE < R: projects earn less than alternatives of similar risk, so pay out all earnings; higher b lowers the price.
ROE = R: the retention ratio does not affect the price.
“Value creation” requires earning more on reinvested capital than investors require for bearing risk.

PVGO.label:
PVGO
Pt = Et+1/R + PVGO
details: Symbols: P<sub>t</sub> = price; E<sub>t+1</sub> = next earnings; R = required return; PVGO = present value of growth opportunities; D<sub>t+1</sub> = next dividend; g = growth rate; b = retention ratio; ROE = return on equity.
Splits the price into assets in place (E<sub>t+1</sub>/R, the no-growth b = 0 value) and growth opportunities: future projects expected to earn more than R.
PVGO = D<sub>t+1</sub>/(R−g) − E<sub>t+1</sub>/R = E<sub>t+1</sub>·b(ROE − R)/[R(R − g)].
With R > g, PVGO > 0 exactly when ROE > R.
ROE > R is a qualitative test; PVGO measures the magnitude, which depends on the gap ROE − R, on b, and on R(R − g). Two firms can both pass the test with very different PVGO.
Because price depends on R − g, small changes in R or g can move the value of growth a lot.

ERISK.label:
How R is set
(asset pricing models)
details: Symbols: R = required return; P<sub>t</sub>, P<sub>t+1</sub> = prices; D<sub>t+1</sub> = next dividend; m<sub>t+1</sub> = SDF; E<sub>t</sub> = expectation at t.
In fixed income, discounting reflected interest-rate risk; for equities the required return reflects systematic risk.
In general P<sub>t</sub> = E<sub>t</sub>[m<sub>t+1</sub>(P<sub>t+1</sub> + D<sub>t+1</sub>)]; the notes formalize R later with asset pricing models.

VRT.label:
Valuation ratios are transformations
of the pricing equation
details: Symbols: D/P = dividend–price ratio (dividend yield); P/E = price–earnings ratio.
D/P and P/E are not arbitrary accounting statistics and not new objects.
Required returns are not directly observable, so ratios are a main tool for studying expected growth, time variation in required returns, and long-horizon return predictability.
The goal is not to label markets over- or undervalued but to read off the expectations embedded in prices.

DPY.label:
Dividend yield
Dt+1/Pt = R − g
details: Symbols: D<sub>t+1</sub> = next dividend; P<sub>t</sub> = price; R = required return; g = growth rate.
Rearranging the GGM.
A low dividend yield means low required returns, high expected growth, or both.
Under this approximation a change in D/P reflects a change in growth expectations or required returns.

DPNOT.label: D/P is NOT merely an income measure
details: It is a summary statistic for discounting and growth expectations.

PE.label:
P/E decomposition
Pt/Et+1 = 1/R + PVGO/Et+1
details: Symbols: P<sub>t</sub> = price; E<sub>t+1</sub> = next earnings; R = required return; PVGO = present value of growth opportunities; ROE = return on equity.
Divide P<sub>t</sub> = E<sub>t+1</sub>/R + PVGO by earnings.
Discount-rate channel: even with PVGO = 0, P/E = 1/R, so a fall in required returns mechanically raises P/E.
Growth channel: growth raises P/E only if reinvested capital earns more than R (ROE > R).
A high P/E may reflect low required returns, valuable growth opportunities, or both.

PENOT.label:
High P/E does NOT necessarily
mean strong growth
details: Symbols: P/E = price–earnings ratio; R = required return.
It may simply reflect low discount rates (the 1/R term).

IMPG.label:
Growth implied by P/E
(P/E)new = ((1+ROEnew)/(1+R))T(P/E)old
details: Symbols: (P/E)<sub>new</sub> = P/E of the growth firm; (P/E)<sub>old</sub> = P/E of a mature firm; ROE<sub>new</sub> = growth firm's ROE; R = required return; T = years of reinvestment; P<sub>0</sub>, P<sub>T</sub> = price now and at T; E<sub>0</sub>, E<sub>T</sub> = earnings now and at T.
Assume the firm reinvests all earnings for T years, then matures and trades at an “old economy” P/E, with R constant.
Then P<sub>0</sub> = P<sub>T</sub>/(1+R)<sup>T</sup> and E<sub>T</sub> = E<sub>0</sub>(1+ROE<sub>new</sub>)<sup>T</sup>; dividing gives the formula, which can be solved for ROE<sub>new</sub>.
The question is not whether prices were “too high” but what expectations were embedded in them.
This isolates the growth channel by holding R fixed; it does not claim ratios are rational or irrational.
IMPG.example: Dot-com, 1999 (Ofek–Richardson 2002): (P/E)<sub>internet</sub> = 605, (P/E)<sub>old</sub> = 30, R = 16%, T = 10 ⇒ ROE<sub>new</sub> ≈ 56.6% a year for a decade. Chan–Karceski–Lakonishok (2002): 98th-percentile 10-year earnings growth 1951–1998 was 31.3%, and survivorship bias pushes that up.

DPLOG.label:
Log dividend–price ratio
dpt = log(Dt/Pt)
details: Symbols: dp<sub>t</sub> = log dividend–price ratio; D<sub>t</sub> = dividend; P<sub>t</sub> = price.
Campbell and Shiller ask: if dp<sub>t</sub> is unusually low (prices high relative to dividends), what must adjust later, dividend growth or returns?

CSD.label:
Campbell–Shiller decomposition
dpt ≈ k + Σρj−1Etrt+j − Σρj−1EtΔdt+j
details: Symbols: dp<sub>t</sub> = log dividend–price ratio; r<sub>t+j</sub> = log return j periods ahead; Δd<sub>t+j</sub> = log dividend growth j periods ahead; ρ = constant slightly below 1 (⚠ not a correlation); k = constant; E<sub>t</sub> = expectation at t; j = periods ahead.
A log-linearization of the present value identity.
r<sub>t+j</sub> is the log return, Δd<sub>t+j</sub> log dividend growth, ρ a constant slightly below one, k a constant from the approximation.

Start from the exact identity P<sub>t</sub> = Σ D<sub>t+i</sub>/Π(1+R<sub>t+s</sub>), which is nonlinear in future returns; take a first-order Taylor expansion around the average dividend–price ratio.
The approximation is accurate in practice because D/P varies within a relatively small range.

CSI.label:
Low D/P ⇒ low future returns
or high future dividend growth
details: Equivalently, high D/P means weak expected growth or high expected returns.
Variation in valuation ratios is the difference between expected future returns and expected future dividend growth.

CSE.label:
Data: dp predicts returns (5–10 yrs),
not dividend growth
details: Symbols: dp<sub>t</sub> = log dividend–price ratio; D/P = dividend yield; P/E = price–earnings ratio.
Beyond one year dp<sub>t</sub> has little power to predict dividend growth; over 5–10 years it strongly predicts returns.
So most variation in valuation ratios historically reflects expected returns, not expected dividend growth.
Same for P/E: a high P/E predicts low future returns, not high future earnings growth.
CSE.example: In 2000 D/P hit a historic low; Shiller testified this implied a real price decline of about 50–55% over the decade if history held. S&P 500: ~1,545 in July 2000, ~800 in July 2002. Recently P/E ≈ 42 (range ~5–44) and D/P ≈ 1.04% (range ~1%–14%).

CAVNOT.label:
Predictability does NOT mean
easy trading profits
details: These are long-horizon (5–10 year) predictions, not short-run forecasts.
Long-horizon forecasts can come with substantial short-run volatility.
The dividend yield has trended down structurally as more firms repurchase shares instead of paying cash.

TVDR.label:
Ratios move with discount rates
(changing Cov with m)
details: Symbols: m = SDF (high m = bad state).
Expected returns are required compensation for risk, set by the covariance of returns with the SDF.
Assets with high returns in bad states (m high) need lower expected returns; high returns in good states need higher ones.
If valuation ratios forecast returns, they forecast time variation in that compensation, i.e. in how returns covary with m.
Explaining why discount rates vary requires modeling uncertainty explicitly, which motivates random variables and probability next.

RV.label:
Random variable
Xt+1 : Ω → ℝ
details: A payoff that depends on which state occurs: Ω is the set of states at t+1 and X<sub>t+1</sub>(ω) is the payoff in state ω.
Anything uncertain at t and realized at t+1 is a random variable: a bond payoff, next period’s dividend, a CDS payoff, a return R<sub>t+1</sub>, the SDF m<sub>t+1</sub>.
Chain: States → Payoffs → Random variables → Expectations → Prices. Random variables let us apply linear operators (expectation, covariance) that determine prices.

SUBJ.label:
Subjective vs objective
probability measure
details: A measure that reflects an investor’s beliefs about which states are more likely is a subjective measure.
The true (objective, physical) measure gives the actual probabilities of states.
We never observe the true measure; investors and econometricians estimate it from data.

MOM.label:
Moments
E[X] = Σ P(ω)X(ω), Var, Std
details: Symbols: ω = a state; P(ω) = probability of state ω (⚠ not a price); X(ω) = payoff in ω; E = expectation; Var = variance; Std = standard deviation.
A probability measure P (P(ω) > 0, Σ P(ω) = 1) induces a distribution over payoffs and defines E, Var and Std.
Var(X) = Σ P(ω)(X(ω) − E[X])<sup>2</sup>; Std = √Var has the same units as X.
The standard deviation of a return is called volatility.

COV.label:
Covariance & correlation
ρX,Y = Cov(X,Y)/(Std X·Std Y)
details: Symbols: X, Y = random variables; ρ<sub>X,Y</sub> = correlation; Std = standard deviation; P(ω) = probability of state ω; a, b = constants; p = probability.
Cov(X,Y) = Σ P(ω)(X(ω) − E[X])(Y(ω) − E[Y]): the strength of the linear relation; in finance, the tendency of two payoffs to be high or low in the same states.
Correlation rescales covariance to −1 ≤ ρ ≤ 1.
If Y = a + bX with b > 0, then ρ = 1 (exercise in the notes).

INFO.label: Information set φ<sub>t</sub>
details: What is known at t: past prices and returns, earnings announcements, macro data, interest-rate moves, any public signal.
Information evolves and prices adjust when news arrives, so expectations and variances are conditional on what is known.

CE.label:
Conditional expectation
Et[Xt+1] ≡ E[Xt+1 | φt]
details: The best forecast of X<sub>t+1</sub> given time-t information: the one that minimizes mean squared forecast error.
It is itself a random variable: its value depends on the information set, and different information gives different forecasts (e.g. high- vs low-growth regime).

CVAR.label:
Conditional variance
Vart(Xt+1) ≡ Var(Xt+1 | φt)
details: Uncertainty that remains after conditioning on what we know now.
It changes when new information arrives, so it is also a random variable.

RATE.label:
Rational expectations
investors’ Et = true E[· | φt]
details: Investors form forecasts with all available information and the correct probability model.
Forecast errors still happen but cannot be systematically predicted with time-t information.

LIE.label:
Law of iterated expectations
Et[Et+1[Xt+2]] = Et[Xt+2]
details: Symbols: E<sub>t</sub> = expectation given time-t information; X<sub>t+2</sub> = variable realized at t+2; φ<sub>t</sub> = information set at t; ⊂ = is contained in.
Holds when information expands over time: φ<sub>t</sub> ⊂ φ<sub>t+1</sub> ⊂ φ<sub>t+2</sub> ….
Your best guess today of your best guess tomorrow is your best guess today.
LIE.example: E<sub>t</sub>[earnings in 2 periods] = 100. A sales report next period is strong (p = 0.75 ⇒ forecast 110) or weak (0.25 ⇒ 70). Check: 0.75·110 + 0.25·70 = 100.

REV.label:
Forecast revisions are unpredictable;
expected forecast error = 0
details: Symbols: E<sub>t</sub>, E<sub>t+1</sub> = forecasts made at t and t+1; X<sub>t+2</sub> = variable being forecast.
E<sub>t</sub>[E<sub>t+1</sub>[X<sub>t+2</sub>] − E<sub>t</sub>[X<sub>t+2</sub>]] = 0.
E<sub>t</sub>[X<sub>t+2</sub> − E<sub>t+1</sub>[X<sub>t+2</sub>]] = 0.

LTV.label:
Law of total variance
Vart = Et[Vart+s] + Vart(Et+s)
details: Symbols: Var<sub>t</sub> = variance given time-t information; E<sub>t+s</sub> = forecast made at the later date t+s; X<sub>t+r</sub> = variable realized at t+r; r > s = horizons.
Var<sub>t</sub>(X<sub>t+r</sub>) = E<sub>t</sub>[Var<sub>t+s</sub>(X<sub>t+r</sub>)] + Var<sub>t</sub>(E<sub>t+s</sub>[X<sub>t+r</sub>]) for r > s ≥ 1.

LTVI.label:
Total risk = news moving forecasts
+ shocks no news predicts
details: Symbols: Var<sub>t</sub>(E<sub>t+s</sub>[X]) = variance of tomorrow's forecast seen from today; E<sub>t</sub>[Var<sub>t+s</sub>(X)] = average uncertainty left after tomorrow's news.
Var<sub>t</sub>(E<sub>t+s</sub>[X]) is variation in forecasts across information states, driven by public information, e.g. strong vs weak early sales data.
E<sub>t</sub>[Var<sub>t+s</sub>(X)] is the average uncertainty left after the best forecast: fundamentally unpredictable shocks such as supply disruptions, legal rulings, macro shocks.

CPR.label:
Prices are conditional
Pt = Et[mt+1Xt+1]
details: Symbols: P<sub>t</sub> = price at t; m<sub>t+1</sub> = SDF; X<sub>t+1</sub> = payoff; E<sub>t</sub> = expectation given time-t information.
The pricing equation has three objects: a random payoff, the SDF, and a conditional expectation.
Prices depend on current information and change as information changes expectations of discounted payoffs.
In equilibrium models conditional expectations describe optimal forecasts; in no-arbitrage models they describe pricing restrictions.

EMH.label:
Efficient Markets
Hypothesis
details: Conditional expectation is the foundation for how information is reflected in prices; the notes return to this with the EMH.
CAPM anomalies raise the central question: do prices fully reflect available information, or do these patterns represent predictable mispricing?

RNI.label:
Risk-neutral investor
max Et[Wt+1]
details: Symbols: W<sub>t</sub> = wealth today; W<sub>t+1</sub> = wealth next period; h = size of the coin-flip gamble; E<sub>t</sub> = expectation at t.
Wealth W<sub>t+1</sub> is a random variable seen from t; a risk-neutral investor cares only about its expectation.
A ±h coin-flip gamble has E[W<sub>t+1</sub>] = W<sub>t</sub> whatever h is, so this investor is indifferent to its size.
RNI.example: W<sub>t</sub> = $100,000: indifferent between $100,000 for sure and $0 or $200,000 with probability ½ each.

MVO.label:
Mean–variance objective
max µp − ½Aσp2
details: Symbols: µ<sub>p</sub> = expected portfolio return; σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> = portfolio variance; A = risk aversion; k = risk penalty on wealth variance; W<sub>t+1</sub> = wealth next period; h = gamble size; R<sub>p</sub> = portfolio return.
Penalize risk: max E<sub>t</sub>[W<sub>t+1</sub>] − k·Var<sub>t</sub>(W<sub>t+1</sub>). k = 0 is risk-neutral, k > 0 risk-averse.
For the ±h gamble Var = h<sup>2</sup>, so the objective is W<sub>t</sub> − kh<sup>2</sup>: any k, h > 0 prefers the certain outcome.
In practice written in returns: µ<sub>p</sub> = E[R<sub>p</sub>], σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> = Var(R<sub>p</sub>), A the risk-aversion parameter, weights summing to 1.
Variance is one possible, and very common, measure of risk.

IC.label:
Indifference curves
ū = µp − ½Aσp2
details: Symbols: ū = fixed utility level; µ<sub>p</sub> = expected portfolio return; σ<sub>p</sub> = portfolio volatility; A = risk aversion.
The objective is called mean–variance utility; an indifference curve is the set of (σ<sub>p</sub>, µ<sub>p</sub>) giving the same utility.
They are used for the graphical solution on the CAL; their shape depends on A.

PARITH.label:
Portfolio arithmetic
µp = Σwiµi, σp2 = ΣΣwiwjσij
details: Symbols: w<sub>i</sub> = portfolio weight on asset i (share of wealth, Σw<sub>i</sub> = 1); µ<sub>i</sub> = E[R<sub>i</sub>], expected return of asset i; σ<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> = Var(R<sub>i</sub>); σ<sub>ij</sub> = Cov(R<sub>i</sub>, R<sub>j</sub>) (σ<sub>ii</sub> = σ<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>); µ<sub>p</sub>, σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> = portfolio expected return and variance; X, Y, Z = random variables, a, b, c = constants. Matrix form: w = column vector of weights, µ = vector of expected returns, G = N×N covariance matrix (entry i,j is σ<sub>ij</sub>), <sup>T</sup> = transpose.
Rules: E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y]; Var(aX + bY) = a<sup>2</sup>Var X + b<sup>2</sup>Var Y + 2ab Cov; Cov(aX + bY, cZ) = ac Cov(X,Z) + bc Cov(Y,Z).
Two assets: σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> = w<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>σ<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> + w<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>σ<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> + 2w<sub>1</sub>w<sub>2</sub>σ<sub>12</sub>.

N assets: σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> = Σ w<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>σ<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> + 2ΣΣ<sub>j>i</sub> w<sub>i</sub>w<sub>j</sub>σ<sub>ij</sub>; in matrix form µ<sub>p</sub> = w<sup>T</sup>µ, σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> = w<sup>T</sup>Gw.
Portfolio variance depends on all pairwise covariances, not just own variances.

MCR.label:
Marginal risk = covariance
∂σp2/∂wk = 2Cov(Rk, Rp)
details: Symbols: σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> = portfolio variance; w<sub>k</sub> = weight on asset k; R<sub>k</sub> = return on asset k; R<sub>p</sub> = portfolio return; σ<sub>k</sub><sup>2</sup> = Var(R<sub>k</sub>); σ<sub>ik</sub> = Cov(R<sub>i</sub>, R<sub>k</sub>); θ<sub>k</sub> = extra amount put in asset k; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate; ∂ = partial derivative.

Differentiate σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> in w<sub>k</sub>: 2(w<sub>k</sub>σ<sub>k</sub><sup>2</sup> + Σ<sub>i≠k</sub> w<sub>i</sub>σ<sub>ik</sub>), which is 2Cov(R<sub>k</sub>, R<sub>p</sub>) by linearity of covariance.
Related identity: σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> = Σ w<sub>i</sub>Cov(R<sub>i</sub>, R<sub>p</sub>), since Cov(R<sub>p</sub>, R<sub>p</sub>) = Var(R<sub>p</sub>).
Assets that covary strongly with the portfolio add the most risk; the idea is central to systematic-risk models like the CAPM.

Finite version: add θ<sub>k</sub> of asset k financed at R<sub>f</sub>: Var[R<sub>p</sub> + θ<sub>k</sub>(R<sub>k</sub> − R<sub>f</sub>)] = σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> + θ<sub>k</sub><sup>2</sup>σ<sub>k</sub><sup>2</sup> + 2θ<sub>k</sub>Cov(R<sub>p</sub>, R<sub>k</sub>) ≈ σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> + 2θ<sub>k</sub>Cov(R<sub>k</sub>, R<sub>p</sub>).

MCRNOT.label:
An asset’s risk contribution is NOT
its own variance in isolation
details: A very volatile asset can add little portfolio risk if it is weakly correlated with the portfolio.

DIV0.label:
Uncorrelated assets
Var(Rp) = σ2/N → 0
details: Symbols: N = number of assets; σ<sup>2</sup> = each asset's variance; R<sub>p</sub> = portfolio return.
Equal weights 1/N, equal variance σ<sup>2</sup>, zero pairwise covariance.
Diversification eliminates portfolio risk in the limit as N grows.

DIVR.label:
Correlated assets
Var(Rp) = σ2/N + (1 − 1/N)ρσ2 → ρσ2
details: Symbols: N = number of assets; σ<sup>2</sup> = each asset's variance; ρ = pairwise correlation; R<sub>p</sub> = portfolio return.
Every pair has correlation ρ > 0, e.g. common exposure to recessions, rates, aggregate demand.
The first term (idiosyncratic) shrinks with N; the second (common movement) stays even in very large portfolios.

SYSR.label:
Idiosyncratic vs systematic risk
only systematic survives diversification
details: Idiosyncratic risk is specific to a security; systematic risk hits many assets at once.
Diversification cancels idiosyncratic shocks but not exposure to common economic forces.
Only systematic risk remains in well-diversified portfolios, so investors require compensation only for systematic risk.

SR.label:
Sharpe ratio
S = (µ − Rf)/σ
details: Symbols: S = Sharpe ratio; µ = expected return; σ = volatility; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.
Expected excess return per unit of volatility.

CAL.label:
Capital allocation line
µp = Rf + S1σp
details: Symbols: µ<sub>p</sub>, σ<sub>p</sub> = portfolio expected return and volatility; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate; w<sub>1</sub> = weight on the risky asset; µ<sub>1</sub>, σ<sub>1</sub> = its expected return and volatility; S<sub>1</sub> = its Sharpe ratio.
One risky asset (µ<sub>1</sub> > R<sub>f</sub>) plus a risk-free asset (variance 0, zero covariance).
µ<sub>p</sub> = R<sub>f</sub> + w<sub>1</sub>(µ<sub>1</sub> − R<sub>f</sub>) and σ<sub>p</sub> = |w<sub>1</sub>|σ<sub>1</sub>: volatility is proportional to the risky share.
Eliminating w<sub>1</sub> (w<sub>1</sub> > 0) gives a straight line in (σ, µ) space with intercept R<sub>f</sub> and slope equal to the Sharpe ratio.
Each extra unit of volatility adds the Sharpe ratio in expected return. Every risky/risk-free mix lies on the CAL.

WSTAR.label:
Optimal risky share
w* = (µ1 − Rf)/(Aσ12) = S1/(Aσ1)
details: Symbols: w<sup>*</sup> = optimal weight on the risky asset; µ<sub>1</sub>, σ<sub>1</sub> = its expected return and volatility; S<sub>1</sub> = its Sharpe ratio; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate; A = risk aversion; w<sub>1</sub> = risky weight.
FOC of max R<sub>f</sub> + w<sub>1</sub>(µ<sub>1</sub> − R<sub>f</sub>) − ½Aw<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>σ<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>.
Separates into a risk-aversion term 1/A and an investment-opportunity term (µ<sub>1</sub> − R<sub>f</sub>)/σ<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>.
All investors hold the same risky asset and scale exposure by risk aversion; this generalizes with many risky assets.
Comparative statics: w<sup>*</sup> rises with expected excess return and falls with variance and with A.

PART.label:
Principle of participation
µ − Rf #gt; 0 ⇒ w* #gt; 0 for every A
details: Symbols: w<sup>*</sup> = optimal risky weight; µ = expected return of the risky asset; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate; A = risk aversion; µ<sub>T</sub> = expected return of the tangency portfolio.
Every mean–variance investor, whatever their risk aversion, holds a positive amount of a risky asset with positive expected excess return.
With many assets: if µ<sub>T</sub> > R<sub>f</sub>, everyone invests something in the tangency portfolio.

TWOR.label:
Two risky assets:
frontier shape set by ρ12
details: Symbols: w<sub>1</sub> = weight on asset 1 (1 − w<sub>1</sub> on asset 2); µ<sub>1</sub>, µ<sub>2</sub> = expected returns; σ<sub>1</sub>, σ<sub>2</sub> = volatilities; ρ<sub>12</sub> = their correlation; µ<sub>p</sub>, σ<sub>p</sub> = portfolio mean and volatility; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.

With w<sub>1</sub> ∈ [0,1]: ρ = 1 gives a straight line from (σ<sub>2</sub>, µ<sub>2</sub>) to (σ<sub>1</sub>, µ<sub>1</sub>), since σ<sub>p</sub> = w<sub>1</sub>σ<sub>1</sub> + (1−w<sub>1</sub>)σ<sub>2</sub>.

ρ = −1 gives two line segments meeting at σ = 0: the assets combine into a risk-free portfolio, so R<sub>f</sub> = µ<sub>2</sub> + (µ<sub>1</sub> − µ<sub>2</sub>)σ<sub>2</sub>/(σ<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>2</sub>), at w<sub>1</sub> = σ<sub>2</sub>/(σ<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>2</sub>).

−1 < ρ < 1: w<sub>1</sub> is linear in µ<sub>p</sub>, so σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> is quadratic in µ<sub>p</sub>: a parabola in (σ<sup>2</sup>, µ), a hyperbola in (σ, µ). Risk is reduced but not eliminated.
Portfolios on the lower part (negative-slope segment, or below the vertex) are mean–variance dominated; optimal portfolios lie on the upper part.

MVF.label:
Minimum-variance frontier
min wTGw s.t. wTµ = µp, wTe = 1
details: Symbols: w = weight vector; G = covariance matrix of returns; µ = vector of expected returns; µ<sub>p</sub> = target portfolio expected return; e = vector of ones, so w<sup>T</sup>e = 1 means weights sum to 1; w<sup>T</sup>Gw = portfolio variance.
For N > 2 risky assets (no risk-free asset): the portfolios with the lowest variance for each expected return.
The frontier has the same shape as the two-asset imperfect-correlation case, but portfolios can now plot inside (to the right of) the curve; those are inefficient.
Approach 1: fix a required µ<sub>p</sub> and solve the constrained minimization for each one.

MVP.label:
Global minimum-variance portfolio
vertex of the frontier
details: Symbols: w<sub>1</sub><sup>*</sup> = weight on asset 1 (asset 2 gets 1 − w<sub>1</sub><sup>*</sup>); σ<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>, σ<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> = variances; σ<sub>12</sub> = Cov(R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>); G = covariance matrix; e = vector of ones.
Lowest possible variance among all portfolios, regardless of expected return.

Two assets: w<sub>1</sub><sup>*</sup> = (σ<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> − σ<sub>12</sub>)/(σ<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> + σ<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> − 2σ<sub>12</sub>). N assets: min w<sup>T</sup>Gw s.t. w<sup>T</sup>e = 1.
MVP.example: Three-asset example (CAPM I): w<sub>MV</sub> = (0.04, 0.32, 0.64), µ = 0.1696, σ = 0.1286, Sharpe 0.9303.

EFR.label:
Efficient frontier of risky assets
upper part of the frontier
details: Symbols: σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> = portfolio variance; w = weight vector; µ = vector of expected returns, so w<sup>T</sup>µ = portfolio expected return.
Lowest variance for a given expected return and highest expected return for a given variance: the part above the vertex.
Approach 2: fix σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> and maximize w<sup>T</sup>µ; this traces only the efficient part.

TAN.label:
Tangency portfolio T
max Sp = (µp − Rf)/σp
details: Symbols: T = tangency portfolio; S<sub>p</sub> = Sharpe ratio of portfolio p; µ<sub>p</sub>, σ<sub>p</sub> = its mean and volatility; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate; w<sub>1</sub><sup>*</sup> = tangency weight on asset 1; µ<sub>1</sub>, µ<sub>2</sub> = expected returns; σ<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>, σ<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> = variances; σ<sub>12</sub> = covariance; w = weight vector; G = covariance matrix; e = vector of ones; w<sub>T</sub>, µ<sub>T</sub>, σ<sub>T</sub>, S<sub>T</sub> = tangency weights, mean, volatility, Sharpe ratio.
With a risk-free asset, any frontier portfolio combines with R<sub>f</sub> along a line whose slope is that portfolio’s Sharpe ratio; T is where the steepest such line touches the frontier.
Highest expected excess return per unit of volatility.

Two assets: w<sub>1</sub><sup>*</sup> = [(µ<sub>1</sub>−R<sub>f</sub>)σ<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> − (µ<sub>2</sub>−R<sub>f</sub>)σ<sub>12</sub>] / [(µ<sub>1</sub>−R<sub>f</sub>)σ<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> + (µ<sub>2</sub>−R<sub>f</sub>)σ<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> − (µ<sub>1</sub>+µ<sub>2</sub>−2R<sub>f</sub>)σ<sub>12</sub>].
Alternative: include R<sub>f</sub>, minimize w<sup>T</sup>Gw s.t. w<sup>T</sup>(µ − eR<sub>f</sub>) = µ<sub>p</sub> − R<sub>f</sub>, then rescale the risky weights to sum to 1.
