TAN.example: CAPM I example (µ = .24/.20/.15, R<sub>f</sub> = .05): µ<sub>p</sub> = 0.1478 gives risky weights (.12, .24, .39), summing to .75; ÷ .75 ⇒ w<sub>T</sub> = (.16, .32, .52), µ<sub>T</sub> = .1804, σ<sub>T</sub> = .1340, S<sub>T</sub> = .9728.

GEF.label:
Global efficient frontier
µp = Rf + STσp
details: Symbols: µ<sub>p</sub>, σ<sub>p</sub> = portfolio mean and volatility; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate; S<sub>T</sub> = Sharpe ratio of the tangency portfolio T.
The straight line through R<sub>f</sub> and T: combinations of the risk-free asset and the tangency portfolio, treating T as a single risky asset.

WTAN.label:
Investor’s share in T
wA = (µT − Rf)/(AσT2)
details: Symbols: w<sub>A</sub> = investor's weight in T; µ<sub>T</sub>, σ<sub>T</sub> = tangency mean and volatility; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate; A = risk aversion; S<sub>T</sub> = tangency Sharpe ratio; w<sub>T</sub> = asset weights inside T.
Same problem as one risky + one risk-free asset, with T as the risky asset; 1 − w<sub>A</sub> goes to the risk-free asset.
Every investor’s portfolio has the same Sharpe ratio S<sub>T</sub>.
Dollar holdings of each risky asset = w<sub>A</sub> × w<sub>T</sub> × wealth.

MFT.label:
Mutual fund theorem
every efficient portfolio = Rf + T
details: Symbols: T = tangency portfolio; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate (here: the risk-free asset).
Tobin (1958); also called the two-fund or Tobin separation theorem.
Investors with the same estimates of means, variances and covariances hold risky assets in the same proportions.
A retirement plan offering a money-market fund and a well-diversified equity fund is fully optimal under certain conditions, and perhaps close enough in general.

MFTNOT.label:
Risk aversion changes how much goes
into T, NOT its composition
details: Conservative investors dilute risky holdings with the risk-free asset but should not change the mix of those risky holdings.

IMPL.label:
Implementing MPT needs
N + N + N(N−1)/2 estimates
details: Symbols: N = number of assets; T = tangency portfolio; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.
Recipe: build the frontier from securities data, find T, choose the mix of T and R<sub>f</sub>.
Difficulties: N expected returns, N variances, N(N−1)/2 covariances; with large N, historical data often suggests a near risk-free portfolio, and the optimizer proposes a large leveraged bet.
Strength: MPT shows how imperfectly, and especially negatively, correlated assets combine to reduce risk.
The estimation burden motivated simplified covariance models such as the single-index model.
IMPL.example: N = 100: 100 expected returns + 100 variances + 4,950 covariances = 5,150 parameters.

SURP.label:
Return surprise
Ri = E[Ri] + ηi, E[ηi] = 0
details: Symbols: R<sub>i</sub> = return on asset i; E[R<sub>i</sub>] = its expected return; η<sub>i</sub> = surprise (unexpected part); σ<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> = its variance.
Split a return into an expected component and an unanticipated “surprise”; Var(η<sub>i</sub>) = σ<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>.
Returns are positively correlated empirically because they share exposure to macro variables: business cycles, interest rates, natural resource prices.

SFM.label:
Single-factor model
Ri = E[Ri] + βiX + εi
details: Symbols: R<sub>i</sub> = return on asset i; X = surprise in the common factor (⚠ not a payoff); β<sub>i</sub> = sensitivity to the factor; ε<sub>i</sub> = firm-specific shock.
X is the unanticipated change in a common macro factor (E[X] = 0); ε<sub>i</sub> is firm-specific, mean zero, uncorrelated with X and across firms.
The common factor generates correlation among returns because all securities respond to the same news.
β<sub>i</sub> lets firms differ in sensitivity: airlines react far more than pharmaceutical firms to an oil price shock.

BETA.label:
Beta
βi = Cov(Ri, RI)/Var(RI)
details: Symbols: β<sub>i</sub> = beta of asset i; R<sub>i</sub> = its return; R<sub>I</sub> = index return.
An asset’s sensitivity (exposure) to the common factor, measured against the index return.
Sensitivity, exposure and loading are synonyms. β is a normalized measure of co-movement with the market portfolio.

SIM.label:
Single-index model
Ri − Rf = αi + βi(RI − Rf) + εi
details: Symbols: R<sub>i</sub> = return on asset i; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate; R<sub>I</sub> = index return; α<sub>i</sub> = alpha (intercept); β<sub>i</sub> = beta; ε<sub>i</sub> = firm-specific shock.

Proxy the factor with a broad market index (Wilshire 5000, Russell 3000, S&P 500): R<sub>i</sub> = E[R<sub>i</sub>] + β<sub>i</sub>(R<sub>I</sub> − E[R<sub>I</sub>]) + ε<sub>i</sub>, then write in excess returns.
α<sub>i</sub> = E[R<sub>i</sub> − R<sub>f</sub>] − β<sub>i</sub>E[R<sub>I</sub> − R<sub>f</sub>].
Taking expectations: E[R<sub>i</sub>] − R<sub>f</sub> = α<sub>i</sub> + β<sub>i</sub>(E[R<sub>I</sub>] − R<sub>f</sub>).
A statistical description of returns, not an equilibrium model.

SIMV.label: σ<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> = β<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>σ<sub>I</sub><sup>2</sup> + σ<sub>ε</sub><sup>2</sup>, Cov(R<sub>i</sub>,R<sub>j</sub>) = β<sub>i</sub>β<sub>j</sub>σ<sub>I</sub><sup>2</sup>
details: Symbols: σ<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> = total variance of asset i; β<sub>i</sub> = beta; σ<sub>I</sub><sup>2</sup> = index variance; σ<sub>ε</sub><sup>2</sup> = idiosyncratic variance Var(ε<sub>i</sub>); R<sub>i</sub>, R<sub>j</sub> = returns of assets i, j.
Total risk = systematic risk + idiosyncratic risk.
Follows because ε’s are uncorrelated with each other and with the index.

WDIV.label:
Well-diversified portfolio
σε,p2 = σε2/N ≈ 0
details: Symbols: R<sub>p</sub> = portfolio return; σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> = its variance; α<sub>p</sub>, β<sub>p</sub>, ε<sub>p</sub> = portfolio alpha, beta, residual; σ<sub>ε,p</sub><sup>2</sup> = portfolio idiosyncratic variance; σ<sub>ε,i</sub><sup>2</sup> = asset i's idiosyncratic variance; σ<sub>I</sub><sup>2</sup> = index variance; R<sub>I</sub> = index return; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate; N = number of assets.

Equal-weighted portfolio: α<sub>p</sub>, β<sub>p</sub>, ε<sub>p</sub> are averages and σ<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup> = β<sub>p</sub><sup>2</sup>σ<sub>I</sub><sup>2</sup> + σ<sub>ε,p</sub><sup>2</sup>, with σ<sub>ε,p</sub><sup>2</sup> = (average σ<sub>ε,i</sub><sup>2</sup>)/N → 0.
Enough securities that idiosyncratic risk is negligible, so R<sub>p</sub> − R<sub>f</sub> ≈ α<sub>p</sub> + β<sub>p</sub>(R<sub>I</sub> − R<sub>f</sub>).
Differences in risk between such portfolios come only from factor exposure. (MPT I used the term loosely; APT will be more precise.)

PARS.label:
302 parameters instead of 5,150
(N = 100)
details: Symbols: N = number of assets.
Single-index inputs: 100 alphas, 100 betas, 100 idiosyncratic variances, 1 expected index return, 1 index variance.

CAPMAS.label: CAPM assumptions
details: Single-period returns; risky assets tradable in perfectly divisible amounts; unlimited borrowing and lending at R<sub>f</sub>.
No taxes or transaction costs; no short-sale constraints.
All investors are mean–variance optimizers with the same beliefs about means, variances and covariances (homogeneous expectations).
Markets clear: supply of each risky asset equals demand.
Several are unrealistic, but they deliver a simple link between expected returns and systematic risk.

MKT.label:
Market portfolio M
all risky assets, value-weighted
details: Symbols: M = market portfolio.
Every risky asset in the economy (stocks, bonds, real estate, art, …) in proportion to its market capitalization (shares outstanding × price).

MKTT.label: Market portfolio = tangency portfolio
details: Symbols: M = market portfolio; T = tangency portfolio; w<sub>T</sub>, w<sub>M</sub> = their asset weights.
Same beliefs ⇒ everyone uses the same mean–volatility diagram and holds mean–variance efficient portfolios.
Mutual fund theorem ⇒ everyone holds the same tangency portfolio.
Markets clear ⇒ investors collectively hold the market portfolio, so M = T, and M is mean–variance efficient.
MKTT.example: Three investors’ demands sum to $9,289 / $18,579 / $30,191 = $58,059 in risky assets; shares 0.16 / 0.32 / 0.52 = w<sub>T</sub>, so w<sub>M</sub> = w<sub>T</sub>.

CML.label:
Capital market line
E[Rp] = Rf + ((E[RM] − Rf)/σM)σp
details: Symbols: R<sub>p</sub>, σ<sub>p</sub> = return and volatility of an investor's portfolio; R<sub>M</sub>, σ<sub>M</sub> = market return and volatility; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.
The line in volatility–expected-return space from the risk-free asset through the market portfolio.
All optimal investor portfolios lie on it.

CAPMR.label:
CAPM: expected return–beta
E[Ri] − Rf = βi(E[RM] − Rf)
details: Symbols: R<sub>i</sub> = return on asset i; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate; R<sub>M</sub> = market return; β<sub>i</sub> = market beta of asset i.
For any return R<sub>i</sub>, with β<sub>i</sub> = Cov(R<sub>i</sub>, R<sub>M</sub>)/Var(R<sub>M</sub>), the loading of asset i on the market return.
A canonical equilibrium model: expected returns are determined by exposure (beta) to market risk, not by standalone variance.
A theoretical statement about expected returns; the time-series regression gives the empirical estimate of β.
Gives an economic interpretation to the single-factor structure of the single-index model.
Although equilibrium is not the course focus, the CAPM is a benchmark for both equilibrium and no-arbitrage approaches.

CAPMNOT.label:
CAPM is a model of expected returns,
NOT a literal pricing formula
details: Despite its name, the CAPM is most often interpreted this way.

APT.label:
APT
(multiple sources of risk)
details: Arbitrage pricing theory is the framework for no-arbitrage pricing models, in contrast to the equilibrium CAPM.
It generalizes the CAPM by allowing multiple sources of risk; the course returns to it later, with a precise definition of well-diversified.

EQTR.label:
Same reward per unit of covariance
(E[Ri] − Rf)/Cov(Ri,RM) equal for all i
details: Symbols: R<sub>i</sub>, R<sub>j</sub>, R<sub>k</sub> = returns of assets i, j, k; R<sub>M</sub> = market return; Δw<sub>k</sub> = small extra weight in asset k (financed at R<sub>f</sub>); R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.

Shift Δw<sub>k</sub> into asset k, financed at R<sub>f</sub>: ΔVar(R<sub>M</sub>) = 2Cov(R<sub>k</sub>, R<sub>M</sub>)Δw<sub>k</sub> and ΔE[R<sub>M</sub>] = Δw<sub>k</sub>(E[R<sub>k</sub>] − R<sub>f</sub>).
Intuitive proof: if asset i’s ratio exceeded j’s, investors would shift toward i and away from j, moving both prices; that cannot persist in equilibrium.

Formal proof: pick Δw<sub>j</sub> = −Δw<sub>i</sub>Cov(R<sub>i</sub>,R<sub>M</sub>)/Cov(R<sub>j</sub>,R<sub>M</sub>) so risk is unchanged. Since M is efficient, the mean cannot change either, which forces the ratios to be equal.
A negative change is ruled out too: reversing the sign of Δw<sub>i</sub> would raise the mean at the same variance.
Setting R<sub>j</sub> = R<sub>M</sub> makes the common ratio (E[R<sub>M</sub>] − R<sub>f</sub>)/Var(R<sub>M</sub>).

QPR.label:
Excess return = quantity × price of risk
βi × (E[RM] − Rf)
details: Symbols: β<sub>i</sub> = market beta of asset i; R<sub>M</sub> = market return; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.
β<sub>i</sub> measures the quantity of market risk; E[R<sub>M</sub>] − R<sub>f</sub> is the price of market risk.

LOWC.label:
Low covariance ⇒ attractive asset
⇒ high price, low expected return
details: An asset with low covariance with the investor’s portfolio tends to pay off when the rest of the portfolio does poorly.
That makes it attractive and lowers its expected return (raises its price) in equilibrium, which motivates beta as the risk measure.

MVEB.label:
Any MV-efficient portfolio gives
a beta representation
details: Symbols: R<sub>p</sub> = return on a mean–variance efficient portfolio; R<sub>i</sub> = return on asset i; β<sub>i,p</sub> = beta of i on p; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.
The proof used only the mean–variance efficiency of the market portfolio.
The full set of equilibrium assumptions is needed only to establish that the market portfolio is efficient.

For efficient R<sub>p</sub>: E[R<sub>i</sub>] − R<sub>f</sub> = β<sub>i,p</sub>(E[R<sub>p</sub>] − R<sub>f</sub>) = Cov(R<sub>i</sub>,R<sub>p</sub>)(E[R<sub>p</sub>] − R<sub>f</sub>)/Var(R<sub>p</sub>).

BEST.label:
Estimating beta
time-series regression on RM,t − Rf,t
details: Symbols: R<sub>i,t</sub> = return on asset i in period t; R<sub>M,t</sub> = market (proxy) return; R<sub>f,t</sub> = risk-free rate; α<sub>i</sub> = alpha; β<sub>i</sub> = beta; ε<sub>i,t</sub> = residual.
R<sub>i,t</sub> − R<sub>f,t</sub> = α<sub>i</sub> + β<sub>i</sub>(R<sub>M,t</sub> − R<sub>f,t</sub>) + ε<sub>i,t</sub>. β<sub>i</sub> is the slope of the fitted line.
R<sub>M,t</sub> − R<sub>f,t</sub> is called a risk factor, and β<sub>i</sub> is the loading on it.
In practice: daily, weekly or monthly data over several years, with a proxy for the market.
BEST.example: Daily 2024 data, S&P 500 as proxy (alpha, beta): Walmart −0.030, 0.398; Aflac −0.031, 0.406; Domino’s −0.011, 0.796.

SBL.label:
SDF beta form
E[Ri] − Rf = βi,m·λm
details: Symbols: R<sub>i</sub> = return on asset i; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate; m = SDF; β<sub>i,m</sub> = beta on m; λ<sub>m</sub> = price of m-risk.
Multiply and divide −Cov(m, R<sub>i</sub>)/E[m] by Var(m).
β<sub>i,m</sub> = Cov(R<sub>i</sub>, m)/Var(m) is the quantity of risk; λ<sub>m</sub> = −Var(m)/E[m] is the price of risk.

CMP.label:
Cov(Ri, m) = −b·Cov(Ri, Rp)
b = E[m](E[Rp] − Rf)/Var(Rp)
details: Symbols: R<sub>i</sub> = return on asset i; m = SDF; R<sub>p</sub> = efficient portfolio return; b = constant linking m and R<sub>p</sub>; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.
Equate the SDF and efficient-portfolio expressions for expected excess returns; holds for all i.
Assets that covary strongly with the efficient portfolio covary strongly, with opposite sign (if E[R<sub>p</sub>] > R<sub>f</sub>), with the SDF.
Both representations say a single underlying source of risk determines all expected excess returns.

MAFF.label:
CAPM as an SDF restriction
m = a − bRM
details: Symbols: m = SDF; a, b = constants; R<sub>M</sub> = market return; R<sub>p</sub> = efficient portfolio return; R<sub>i</sub> = return on asset i.

From Cov(R<sub>i</sub>, m + bR<sub>p</sub>) = 0 for all i: if any payoff can be replicated with traded assets, a variable with zero covariance with every traded return must be constant, so m + bR<sub>p</sub> = a.
The SDF is affine in the efficient portfolio’s return; under CAPM that portfolio is the market.
CAPM can be viewed as a restriction on the SDF.

CORRM.label: Corr(m, R<sub>M</sub>) = −1
details: Symbols: m = SDF; R<sub>M</sub> = market return; Corr = correlation.
Algebraically immediate once m is affine in R<sub>M</sub>.
High R<sub>M</sub> (good states) means low m; low R<sub>M</sub> (bad states) means high m.

ONED.label:
All priced risk is one-dimensional,
captured by the market portfolio
details: Symbols: R<sub>M</sub> = market return.
R<sub>M</sub> captures all pricing-relevant variation in the SDF, which is why one factor can price all assets.
This is the model’s real economic content; the correlation of −1 is only the algebra.

BFROMM.label: Beta form ⇔ SDF affine in R<sub>p</sub>
details: Symbols: m = SDF; a, b = constants; R<sub>p</sub> = efficient portfolio return; R<sub>i</sub> = return on asset i; β<sub>i</sub>, β<sub>p</sub> = betas on R<sub>p</sub>; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.
Substitute m = a − bR<sub>p</sub> into E[m(1 + R<sub>i</sub>)] = 1 and use E[m] = 1/(1 + R<sub>f</sub>): E[R<sub>i</sub>] − R<sub>f</sub> = β<sub>i</sub>(1 + R<sub>f</sub>)b·Var(R<sub>p</sub>).
Applied to R<sub>p</sub> itself (β<sub>p</sub> = 1) this gives E[R<sub>p</sub>] − R<sub>f</sub> = (1 + R<sub>f</sub>)b·Var(R<sub>p</sub>), hence the beta form.
Expected excess returns are determined by covariance with a single portfolio if and only if the SDF is affine in that portfolio’s return.
The step-by-step expansion is marked optional in the notes.

PRR.label:
λm #lt; 0 matches a positive
market risk premium
details: Symbols: λ<sub>m</sub> = price of m-risk; m = SDF; b = loading of m on the market; R<sub>M</sub> = market return.
λ<sub>m</sub> is negative because assets that covary positively with m pay off in bad states and so have low expected returns.
Under CAPM Var(m) = b<sup>2</sup>Var(R<sub>M</sub>), and covariance with m is proportional, with opposite sign, to covariance with R<sub>M</sub>.
Changes in the market risk premium reflect how strongly the SDF loads on the market return.

SML.label:
Security market line
E[R] against β, slope E[RM] − Rf
details: Symbols: E[R] = expected return; β = market beta; R<sub>M</sub> = market return; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate; µ = expected return.
The expected return–beta relation drawn in (β, µ) space.
Under CAPM all assets lie on an upward-sloping SML.

ALPHA.label: CAPM prediction: all α<sub>i</sub> = 0
details: Symbols: α<sub>i</sub> = alpha (regression intercept) of asset i; β<sub>i</sub> = beta; R<sub>i</sub>, R<sub>M</sub> = asset and market returns; R<sub>f</sub> = risk-free rate.
Any deviation from the SML equals the regression intercept α.
Taking expectations of the regression gives E[R<sub>i</sub>] − R<sub>f</sub> = α<sub>i</sub> + β<sub>i</sub>(E[R<sub>M</sub>] − R<sub>f</sub>).

GRS.label:
GRS test
joint test that all alphas are zero
details: Gibbons–Roll–Shanken hypothesis test.
Early tests were not a great success: average returns against individual-stock betas show a lot of dispersion, and the best-fitting line is too flat to pass through a plausible risk-free rate.
Individual stock returns are so volatile that you cannot reject that all average returns are the same, which gives the test low power.

SORT.label:
Sort stocks into portfolios
⇒ higher test power
details: Portfolios have lower idiosyncratic variance and more stable betas, so differences in average returns can be distinguished.
Fama–MacBeth (1973) and Black–Jensen–Scholes (1972) formed portfolios on estimated betas, then estimated portfolio betas in the following period.
Portfolios have since been formed on size, book/market, industry and other characteristics.
Procedure: pick a characteristic, sort stocks on it, estimate portfolio betas and average returns, plot the SML.

ANOM.label:
Anomalies: value, size,
momentum, reversal
details: Value: high book-to-market stocks earn high returns relative to the CAPM prediction.
Size: small stocks earn somewhat higher returns.
Momentum: stocks that did well over the past year earn high subsequent returns.
Reversal: stocks that did well over the past 3–5 years earn low returns.

ANOMI.label: Mispricing or missing risk?
details: Possible readings: markets may not fully reflect available information, or a more general model of risk and return is needed.

ROLL.label:
Roll critique
any test is a joint test with the proxy
details: Symbols: R<sub>M</sub> = return on the true market portfolio.
Roll (1977): the true market portfolio includes all risky assets, human capital too, but practice uses proxies such as stock indices.
The CAPM cannot be tested without observing the true market portfolio.
A test is jointly of the CAPM and of whether the proxy for R<sub>M</sub> is correct, so a failure may be the model or the measurement.
The notes conclude that the CAPM itself can never be rejected.

ONEF.label:
No single portfolio explains the
cross section ⇒ multiple factors
details: Shift the question from the right proxy to whether any traded portfolio captures all priced risk.
Empirically none appears to, which suggests priced risk is not one-dimensional.

BENCH.label: CAPM is best viewed as a benchmark
details: Empirical tests give mixed support: many assets have non-zero alphas, and several anomalies are inconsistent with the CAPM.
Its value lies in showing how strong restrictions on the SDF translate into sharp predictions about expected excess returns.
